summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: We tried popular Hunts Chinese restaurant and it brought so much flavour
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Cambridgeshire food reviewer Lucy Melton shares her thoughts following a recent visit to a popular Chinese restaurant in St Ives At the weekend I did something I haven’t done in years – went to a Chinese restaurant! Don’t get me wrong, I’ll have a takeaway every now and then, but it’s been years since I actually went to a restaurant and I’d forgotten how good it can be. We headed to The Welcome in St Ives, which has been around for years and has always had a good reputation. We decided to go for the à la carte menu over the buffet and it actually worked out cheaper. We had SO much food and even ended up taking some home. Selection of dishes (Image: Lucy Melton) I started with the chicken and sweetcorn soup, the thick broth and flavour were delicious, and it’s such a great way to start. We also had the chicken satay skewers, which were great, with loads of meat and plenty of flavour. Chicken Satay (Image: Lucy Melton) We had so much food but my highlights were the chicken in yellow bean sauce, a dish I hadn’t had before and I’m so glad I tried it. The Hong Kong style sweet & sour was really good too, it wasn’t too sickly, which I was thankful for, and it had crispy chicken, which is my favourite. The duck had amazing flavour, as did the shredded chilli beef, which had the perfect crunch to it. Shredded chilli beef (Image: Lucy Melton) The king prawn noodles were a massive portion as was the house special fried rice with garlic and soy sauce; you got so much meat, and both were great! King prawn noodles (Image: Lucy Melton) House fried rice (Image: Lucy Melton) The deep fried prawns were another highlight, big prawns inside, the batter was cooked really well and they came with a great sauce to dip them in. Honestly, I’d forgotten how much I enjoy sitting down and having a proper Chinese meal. So much food and loads of variety, I won't leave it as long next time!

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Cambridgeshire bus services to change after combined authority review
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A number of bus services in Cambridgeshire are due to change following a review. Cambridgeshire and Peterborough Combined Authority (CPCA) carried out a review of bus services across the county to ensure the bus network was affordable, sustainable, evidence led and better aligned to passenger need. In Peterborough, the proposed changes include merging services 60 and 61, and introducing different timetables for services 60, 61, 62 and 63. They also include retaining the current loop around Werrington as part of the 62 service, helping residents to continue accessing Werrington centre. Service 60 runs between Peterborough Queensgate Bus Station and Orton Northgate, while 61 runs between Queensgate and Newark Sainsbury’s, 62 runs between Queensgate and Maxey, and 63 runs between Queensgate and Parnwell. A report to go before the CPCA transport committee on September 9 stated: “There would be no significant change to overall service levels [in Peterborough], but the network should be simpler to operate and explain.” The revised proposals were developed in response to a six-week public consultation that received 1,182 responses. Residents emphasised the need for reliability, punctuality, frequency, operating hours, access to rail and healthcare, the need for clear information, affordability and integrated ticketing, and the importance of services that were usable for work, education, healthcare, shopping and leisure. If approved at next week’s meeting, the changes could be introduced from February 2027, with further changes planned for August 2027. CPCA Mayor Paul Bristow said: “Thank you to everyone who took the time to share their views as part of our Bus Network Review. “Listening to residents is incredibly important, because you are the people who use these services and understand what works well and where improvements are needed.” Fenland – Services 46, 50, 56 and Tiger 7 would be redesigned to create a clearer local network, including improved March–Wisbech links, better weekend provision and revised connections through Chatteris. St Ives, Earith, Somersham and Ramsey –  The 301 would be improved to provide a simpler, more frequent core service, with Tiger 12 withdrawn alongside replacement links and implementation planning. St Neots, Godmanchester, the Hemingfords and St Ives – Service 65 would be revised to serve St Neots Rail Station and extend from the Offords to Godmanchester, the Hemingfords and St Ives. Cambridge and South Cambridgeshire – Services including 8, 26, 27, 27A, 27H, 75, T2, T4 and T5 would be revised to improve reliability, provide more regular Cambridge links and support evening, weekend and peak-time travel. East Cambridgeshire and Suffolk links –  Several existing low-frequency services around Haverhill and Newmarket would be replaced by simpler services, including new 119, 120 and 121 routes.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Cambridgeshire ‘school streets’ could be enforced with cameras
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Cambridgeshire County Council is considering the use of cameras to enforce school streets. School streets restrict car movements at drop-off and pick-up times to reduce pollution and encourage walking and other active travel methods. Cambridgeshire County Council’s highways and transport committee was asked to approve a report detailing their approach to using cameras to enforce traffic rules. They were told that “initial planning work” has started on installing Automatic Number Plate Recognition (ANPR) cameras to enforce turning restrictions on roads such as Downing Street. Council officers also said they had started looking into using the cameras to enforce school streets, but these would need further assessment before being approved. Cllr Darren Green, of Romsey, said he was “very, very happy” that the council was considering this. The Green councillor said: “We know already that school streets can be very fragile and rely on a lot of volunteer work and best practice would be to back this all up with a camera system. “I hope going forward, once this is in place, that we can prioritise using cameras on school streets.” Cllr Alex Beckett, chair of the committee, stressed that volunteers would still be important regardless of if the cameras had been installed. The Liberal Democrat councillor said: “When the general public see that there are actually members of the community willing to stand up and man the school streets, and protect that school, it has a much better impact that having a no-name camera that feels a bit like it’s the state doing it, or the council doing it, when actually most school streets are really supported by the parents and those there. “I think wherever possible I would support the use of volunteers on school streets but I do know that is increasingly challenging in some places. “In some places unfortunately the level of harassment that is given to those school streets volunteers means the cameras might be a better approach.”

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Free blood pressure checks at Huntingdon surgery as part of national campaign
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Huntingdon residents are being offered free blood pressure checks at Priory Fields Surgery on September 8 as part of a national campaign to identify the potentially dangerous condition. Priory Fields Surgery in Huntingdon is supporting Know Your Numbers Week by offering a free, drop-in blood pressure session on Tuesday, September 8 from 12.30pm to 2pm. High blood pressure, which affects around 14.4 million adults in England, is often undiagnosed and can lead to serious health problems. Dr Chris Smith from Priory Fields Surgery said: "High blood pressure is often called a silent risk because it rarely comes with obvious symptoms or warning signs. "However, leaving it unchecked over time significantly increases your risk of experiencing a stroke or heart attack later in life, and it can also quietly damage your kidneys. "The good news is that checking your numbers is quick, simple and straightforward. "Taking a few moments to get it checked gives you a clear picture of where you stand, helping you protect your long-term health before any harm is done." An estimated 5.5 million people are living with undiagnosed high blood pressure in England. The surgery, located on Nursery Road, is also encouraging residents to register with a GP if they have not already done so. Registration is available online at prioryfieldssurgery.nhs.uk/practice-information/new-patients.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Cambs man who filmed himself sexually assaulting sleeping woman jailed
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A Cambridgeshire man who filmed himself sexually assaulting a sleeping woman has been jailed. Kenan Samuel, 28, invited the victim and a male friend to his home in Alconbury Weald, near Huntingdon, for drinks on December 18, 2020. After the victim fell asleep, Samuel got into bed with her and touched her without consent. He filmed the assault while the victim was unconscious and unable to consent. Detective Constable Sally Muntane-Crane, who investigated the case, said: "Samuel is a dangerous man who took advantage of the victim when she was in a vulnerable state. Kenan Samuel "He was also cunning, deleting the evidence he had sent himself a nude photo from the victim’s phone without her consent." Police seized and examined Samuel’s phone after the victim reported the assault. Officers found he had sent himself a nude photograph from the victim’s phone, then deleted the message to cover his tracks. Samuel, of Lysons Close, was sentenced at Peterborough Crown Court on Friday, August 28, after admitting to assault by penetration, voyeurism, and causing a computer to perform a function to secure unauthorised access to data. He was jailed for five years. Det Con Muntane-Crane said: "I would like to praise the victim for reporting what happened, and for showing tremendous strength and bravery during the investigation. "I hope it gives confidence to other victims to come forward, knowing they will be listened to, and the police and wider criminal justice system will do everything they can to get justice for them." Further information and support concerning consent can be found on the police website.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Ex-teacher slams school's uniform rule as pupils face isolation over haircuts
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary:
A Huntingdonshire school has apologised after children who opted for certain hairstyles risked being placed in isolation. Longsands Academy, in St Neots, told parents that students would be placed in "reset" if their haircut or hair colour was not deemed to be an acceptable style. According to the school's recently updated uniform policy, "harsh or dramatic contrast between the top of the hair and the sides" is banned. Patterns shaved into a scholar's hair or eyebrows, including an artificial parting, and "high or flamboyant hairstyles" are also outlawed. Meanwhile, skin fades where the pupil's hair is below a grade one and hair that is "teased, backcombed or covered in excessive product" are prohibited. For girls, hair "must be in a conventional and understated style" with hair clips or hair bands either "black or navy blue" in colour. Styles involving large bunches, buns or ponytails on top of the head "obscuring the views of pupils sitting behind" are banned. Under the rule, pupils would remain in isolation until parents grant permission for them to visit a hairdresser to have the hairstyle "rectified". The strict measure sparked a backlash among parents, with people describing the diktat as "concerning". Read more Cambs paedophile, 67, told young girl 'not to tell anyone' about sexual activity
    New 3G football pitch approved despite fears it would make noise problem worse
    Seven NHS children angle a catch at fishing lake
    Boy, three, injured in crocodile enclosure at Cambs zoo discharged from hospital
    Hunts zoo hosts exclusive after-hours event for children and families A former teacher at Longsands, who asked to remain anonymous, claimed the policy is "highly focussed on the ethnic minority population". They told The Hunts Post: "It is worrying that they are allowed to even suggest such requirements of students to all look a clone of one another and not celebrate difference. "The school has taken a significant directional shift since I was there. Focusing more on the policing of children than the teaching and ensuring learning is exciting. "With the booklet learning and scripted narrative, the policy around policing hair styles doesn’t surprise me - what does is the heavily racial focus of such a policy. "I think this policy, being so heavily drawn to focus on minorities could see for a significant rise in racial issues." Longsands Academy in St Neots is run by the Astrea Academy Trust (Image: Street View) The ex-teacher added the policy "removes individualisation and celebrates difference, diversity and culture." It also focuses "a lens on minority groups as being ‘other’ and needing to conform to fit in. This is not the message a school should be sending youth of today," they said. Meanwhile, one parent has taken aim at an illustration of six pupils with hair styles deemed "inappropriate" which accompanies the school's uniform policy. Of the six images featured, four appear to depict students from an ethnic minority background. "I find this concerning because it raises questions about how the policy was developed and whether the examples being used are fair and representative," they said. "Hair can have important cultural and ethnic significance, and policies concerning hairstyles need to be applied consistently and sensitively to all pupils." The parent added they have also sought clarification on how the police applied to pupils who are non-binary. A spokesperson for Astrea Academy Trust, which runs Longsands Academy, said: "We have recently updated our uniform policy to reduce the number of branded items students are required to have this academic year. "As part of this, we updated our haircut policy with illustrations to make clear the sorts of patterns that are not acceptable. “We have listened carefully to the views of parents who told us that these illustrations suggested that certain hairstyles such as cornrows were banned, which was not our intention. "We have worked closely with parents and carers and apologise that the policy was not clear." They added: "We will be sending out an update for families and students shortly. We would also like to thank parents who have contacted us and engaged so positively with us. “We are an inclusive school and we recognise and celebrate our staff and student identities from all backgrounds. "We strongly encourage parents to contact us directly about any concerns they have, rather than our social media pages, which are not frequently monitored." Have you got a story you want to share? summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: 'Dangerous' abuser bit and kicked ex-partner in vicious attack
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A man who attacked his ex-partner and continually breached a restraining order has been jailed. James Upton was handed the restraining order in March 2024, banning him from contacting his former partner or visiting her home in St Neots for five years. The 26-year-old breached the order by making multiple attempts to contact the victim by phone and turned up at her house on different occasions. During one of those visits, in February 2024, an argument broke out between the pair which quickly became physical. Upton, of Coventry Road, Bedford, pushed the victim to the floor, biting her, and kicking her in the stomach. He also damaged the victim’s iPhone, smashing the screen. He was arrested and charged with ABH and four counts of harassment - breach of restraining order, which he admitted. At Peterborough Crown Court on Friday August 28, Upton was jailed for one year and five months after the activation of the previous suspended sentence. DC Madie Mayers-Brandrith, who investigated, said: “Upton is a very dangerous individual, who shows no regard for the law and the restrictions imposed on him by the courts. "To attack his former partner in her own home when the pair’s young son was present is despicable so I am pleased Upton will now serve time behind bars for his actions.” Have you got a story you want to share? summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Job with The Co-operative Bank returned my confidence after Centerpoint support
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A young person who experienced homelessness says a job with The Co-operative Bank returned his ‘confidence’. Michael, spent most of his life in care. However, after he returned home from university his relationship broke down with his foster parents – forcing him into sofa surfing and eventually on to the streets. After a few months, he got in contact with Centrepoint, who were able to place him into accommodation and help him find a job. It was here that Michael started working at The Co-operative Bank, through it’s Brick by Brick scheme, and he hasn’t looked back since. He said: “Over two years I applied for 400 jobs. It was demoralising because I really wanted to work but couldn’t as employers would either say I was too experienced or not experienced enough. “Thankfully, Centrepoint and The Co-operative Bank were able to support me into this job now and I love it. Everyone’s friendly and supportive and it’s given me a purpose, as opposed to just existing.” Brick by Brick, launched earlier this year, is a pioneering early careers programme, designed to support young people into sustainable work and move on from homelessness for good. It provides a steady, structured journey starting with employability workshops, and then progressing to the Get Set Go Programme which provides six days classroom learning, mock interviews, professional behaviour guidance, and an introduction to the Bank’s values. After this, a young person will then complete work experience at the Bank which, if successful, is followed by an employment offer, removing the pressure of formal interviews. The program ends with an optional apprenticeship and keep in touch days, designed to improve preparedness between a job offer and start date. The initiative has had 35 young people participating in various steps so far with several securing permanent employment in the Bank’s Contact Centre. Michael is one of these, and discussing the skills it has given him, he said: “Communication, multitasking, timekeeping, but most importantly, confidence. “I’ve gone from thinking ‘Why would a company want me’ to now thinking ‘Why wouldn’t they’.” With over one million young people currently not in education or employment, Brick by Brick is reshaping conversations about homelessness by refusing to define young people by their experiences, instead investing in their potential and honouring their needs. “By meeting young people where they’re at, we can close the opportunity gap that holds too many back from reaching their potential,” said Anna Cuskin, the Bank’s Social Impact Lead. “Everyone deserves the chance to succeed. With the right support, young people can gain confidence, find meaningful employment and build a future beyond homelessness.” A man who was at risk of homelessness has told us how a new home gave him a ‘sense of purpose.’ Kai, 22, was living with his dad before overcrowding at home forced him to find somewhere else to live, he said: “It was a really worrying time. I didn’t know where to go or who to turn to.” Fortunately, Kai was able to get in contact with Centrepoint where through the Rent Deposits Scheme, funded by Nationwide Building Society, he was able to find a place in a House In Multiple Occupation (HMO). “It’s given me the stability to rebuild my life and slowly I'm getting back on track. “One day I'd like to live in a house of my own, by a river, on my own plot of land, and do what I want with it. “That’s my dream and I feel like if I keep sticking at it, I’ll be able to eventually achieve it.” However, young people in Kai’s situation may not be so fortunate – research by Centrepoint has found there has been a 10% fall in HMOs since 2019, with 458,000 in 24/25 compared to 510, 776 in 19/20. When asked if he had any advice for young people going through something similar, Kai said: “Don't give up. It might be hard, but right now, your best bet is to keep pushing forward and look for any form of help where you possibly can. Just keep going.” (Image: Centrepoint) The Prime Minister’s pledge to end rough sleeping has been given an early boost after the number of young people sleeping rough in London dropped by almost half. Between April and June 2026, 202 18–25-year-olds in London were recorded as sleeping rough. This was a 45% decrease from the same quarter last year when 368 young people were reported. The youth homelessness charity Centrepoint said this was cause for celebration and called the number proof that the Prime Minister’s pledge could be achieved. Lisa Doyle, the charity’s Head of Policy and Public Affairs, said: “London is providing the blueprint for what can be achieved when political leaders has the vision and intent to end street homelessness. “These figures are a real cause for celebration, but the job is not done. The Mayor of London and the Government must continue these efforts until rough sleeping is reduced to as close to zero as possible, and anyone forced onto the streets is helped off them quickly. However, the charity warned that ending street sleeping alone is not enough. “We must also remember that homelessness does not begin and end with rough sleeping.” Lisa said, “For every person on the streets, many thousands more are living in insecure or unsafe situations. To avoid reversing this positive trend, the Government must now also address the causes and consequences of those experiences too, and step up efforts to prevent homelessness.” A charity has warned that homeless people’s lives are ‘at risk’ due to the past few months of high temperatures. It comes after August saw another flurry of heatwaves – regularly rising over 30 degrees across the country. The UK’s leading youth homelessness charity, Centrepoint, believes council should do more to protect those sleeping rough when it’s this hot. Lisa Doyle, Head of Policy and Public Affairs, said: “This weather is life threatening for those forced to sleep on the streets. “And while many councils do activate protocols to protect those sleeping rough, there is no legal requirement for local authorities to provide shelter for everyone during severe weather. This must change.” “Ultimately, street homelessness is just the tip of the iceberg – the best way to keep people safe is to reduce homelessness however it is experienced.”

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Vape related blazes cost Cambs fire service more than £850 in just three years
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary:
Vape-related fires have cost Cambridgeshire Fire & Rescue Service more than £850 in just three years, new data reveals. Recent figures show that in the county alone, three such incidents between 2023 and 2025 have cost the fire service £851.85 in call-out fees, with most of the expense incurred in 2025. The data was released by Cambridge waste collection experts at BusinessWaste.co.uk, following Freedom of Information requests. Mark Hall, commercial waste specialist at BusinessWaste.co.uk, said: "The sharp rise in fires involving vapes is extremely concerning to all parties involved. "Almost £58,000 has been spent by just three fire services, and that covers only the immediate cost of attending these incidents. "It does not include the damage a fire can cause to a bin lorry, waste facility, home or business. "While we do not have a wider picture of the costs across the country, it’s especially worrying as these continue to grow throughout the year. "This shows how quickly the costs can grow when vapes are thrown away incorrectly and how a small disposal mistake can create a much larger public cost." summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: The fascinating history of St Ives island's basket makers
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Keith Grimwade, Chair of the Friends group, describes the willow-weaving heritage of Holt Island Nature Reserve Osiers, the type of willow used for weaving, were grown on Holt Island from the 1720s to the 1920s. They give the island its name – ‘Holt’ is a local word for a plantation, especially an osier plantation. There was a big demand for willow wands (also known as ‘withies’ or ‘rods’) to make different types of baskets, and products such as filters for fire engine hoses and sieves for straining fruit in jam factories. In 1877 John Harrison founded ‘Harrison and Son, Willow Growers and Basket Makers of St Ives’. The firm prospered and became one of the largest growers of willow in the country. It had several osier plantations along the river, including Holt Island, and totalling 45 acres. Harrisons developed their own hybrid willow, ideal for basket work, a cross between Salix viminalis and Salix triandra. The willow wands were cut by men over the winter. In the spring the firm employed 70-80 women to remove the bark from the wands – ‘stripping the willow’, a call you may have heard when country dancing! From March to June men were employed to hoe between the lines of osiers. The willow wands on Holt Island were sorted, bundled and then taken by barge to The Quay, downstream of the town bridge. It was then transported by horse and cart to the Harrison’s workshop in Filbert’s Walk (now demolished). John’s son Charles, and then his grandson Jack, followed him into the business. One of their biggest contracts was making the sorting baskets for the Post Office. This was ‘square work’, which is much more difficult than making a round basket. The business closed in 1970, unable to compete with the introduction of plastic. But by then they had made over 30,000 potato baskets! Jack described basket making ‘as a work of art’. Fortunately, there are still people who have learnt, and pass on, this ancient skill. Join us on Holt Island on Heritage Open Day on Saturday, 12th September, when John Conkey of the British Basket Makers Association will be demonstrating traditional basket-making techniques from 10.30 am to 3 pm. There may be a chance for you to have a go at weaving, too. We will also have a display of Harrison baskets, kindly lent to us by Jack’s daughter, Charlotte.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: DVLA £1,000 fine warning ahead of change coming to UK roads today
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Drivers are being urged to make sure their number plates are road legal as the new “76” vehicle registration number hits UK roads. Motorists in England, Scotland and Wales will see the new number plates on the road when they are released today. They must make sure their own number plates adhere to specifications in order to be road legal, with a warning that those that do not comply with rules could be hit with a £1,000 fine. The Driver and Vehicle Licensing Agency (DVLA) is reminding drivers to check their own plates meet the required specifications. Plates that do not comply can lead to a fine and an MOT failure. The DVLA said: “Number plates (also known as licence plates) must show your registration number correctly. You cannot rearrange letters or numbers, or alter them so that they’re hard to read. "You could be fined up to £1,000 and your vehicle will fail its MOT test if you drive with incorrectly displayed number plates." These are the rules you should be aware of around licence plates from the DVLA. The number plates on your vehicle must: The characters must not be removable or reflective. If your number plates were fitted after 1 September 2021, they must also be a single shade of black. Your number plates can also: Graham Conway, Managing Director at Select Car Leasing , said: “Characters must not be removable or reflective, however, your number plates can have 3D (raised) characters, display certain flags, symbols and identifiers and display a green flash, if you have a zero-emission vehicle. “It’s important to drivers to understand the nuances of what’s required for their licence plates as even the smallest modifications could make it illegal. For example, 3D characters are allowed on licence plates, but if the raised letters are not black or have a reflective coating on them, this could make them illegal. Recommended Reading: “It’s also important for drivers to understand that any modifications around their licence plate, that could make it unreadable, are also considered illegal. “For example, licence plate lights must be white – not tinted blue or any other colour – and need to illuminate the plate evenly without causing any shadows. The bulbs themselves must not be visible. “Failure to meet these requirements can result in fines of up to £1,000, as well as an MOT failure for the vehicle. “Motorists looking to replace or customise their plates should only buy from DVLA-registered suppliers who follow the legal guidelines. Plates that feature illegal fonts, incorrect spacing, tinted backgrounds, or missing supplier information can all lead to penalties. “For those unsure whether their plates comply, checking with a reputable supplier or consulting DVLA guidelines is the safest way to avoid unnecessary fines or complications.”

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: 'Reckless' man who stabbed victim for ringing bell on e-scooter pictured
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A man has been jailed for a stabbing outside a kebab shop in Peterborough city centre - after another customer rang the bell on his e-scooter. Kris Stimson, 44, was at the takeaway in Fitzwilliam Street at about 2.30am on June 20 last year when he became enraged after hearing the bell being used. Mistakenly believing it was the victim, an argument ensued outside. He produced a knife and stabbed the man in the abdomen, before leaving the scene and discarding the weapon behind some locked gates in Geneva Street. Armed police found Stimson nearby and had to use incapacitant spray to arrest him. Members of the public attempted to stem the victim’s bleeding, before paramedics arrived and he was taken to hospital for treatment. A cordon was put in place, and officers recovered the weapon following Stimson’s attempts to hide it. Whilst in custody, Stimson enquired about whether the man had died. The victim underwent surgery, was placed in an induced coma and required further treatment for several weeks before being discharged. Stimson, of Greenham, Bretton, Peterborough, admitted assault causing grievous bodily harm without intent and possession of a knife in public. On Friday (August 28) at Cambridge Crown Court he was jailed for 16 months. DC John Pentney said: “Stimson’s shocking actions were completely disproportionate for something as trivial as the bell being used on his scooter. "Stabbing someone like this is extremely reckless and we could easily have been dealing with a murder investigation. "I would like to commend the members of the public who stemmed the victim’s bleeding while waiting for paramedics to arrive. "Their actions could well have contributed to him surviving." summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Drivers warned simple parking mistake could leave them with £1,200 repair bill
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: The last few months has seen some extreme weather in the UK from heatwaves to droughts and now drivers are being warned about the weather’s effect on trees. That’s because it’s easy to park under a tree and expect no damage to be done to your car, but you could get into some bother if a branch comes loose and lands on it. With the sun still making an appearance, you might choose to park under a tree to keep your car cool, but you’ll need to be aware of the risk of branches breaking without warning, says Graham Conway, managing director at Select Car Leasing. He says a falling tree branch can cause serious damage to a car and risk injuring a driver or passengers. Conway added: “In the hot weather, it’s understandable that motorists will look for any shady spot to park their car to try and keep it cooler. “But with prolonged dry, hot weather, tree branches may be weakened and break without warning.” He explains: “Falling branches, particularly from large trees, can cause significant structural damage to a car, which could cost motorists thousands. “Heavy branches could dent the body, shatter the windscreen or break side mirrors. “Even damage from smaller branches can result in dents and scratches to the body of the car. “Look out for trees that have grey, brittle wood or bark that is peeling off, as this is often a sign that the tree is dying, causing the branches to dry out and snap off. “Trees that have cracks or splits, especially at the point where a branch joins the trunk, may also indicate that a tree is dying. “However, there aren’t always warning signs, so it’s best to be extra cautious.” He said trees can also experience ‘summer branch drop syndrome’, which can happen without visible signs. Conway added: “This most often occurs when sudden summer rain follows a long, dry period. “Insurance will typically cover any damage as a result of an ‘act of God’ however, if the tree was on council or private land and was already in a dangerous state, you may be able to recover your excess costs from whoever owns it. “If the tree was clearly deteriorating before it fell, or the owner had been warned and failed to act, they could be considered negligent. “If you think the owner was at fault, photograph the tree's condition, keep any evidence, and raise it with your insurer.” “As a guide, UK bonnet repairs can range from around £50 to £150 for minor dents, £300 to £700 for a replacement bonnet and £500 to £1,200+ for major structural damage, while comprehensive car insurance can cover falling trees and branches during storms, depending on the policy.” Smith added: “Drivers should also be careful about parking under trees during windy or wet weather, as weakened branches may not be obvious from ground level. “If a storm is forecast, it is always better to move the car somewhere more open, even if that means walking a little further.” Recommended reading: The expert adds that there are a few more things you should bear in mind when parking under a tree: Smith explains: “Sap and droppings in particular can mark the paintwork, and if they are baked on by the sun, they can become much harder to remove without causing scratches.” He also shared some more spots you should think twice about parking close to: He said you can expect an increased risk of debris, dust or accidental damage or a bigger chance of dents, scratches or broken windows in these areas. Concluding, he advises drivers to be aware of where they are parking: “The safest approach is to look up and around before leaving your car. “If there is anything above, beside or nearby that could fall, blow over, leak, mark the paintwork or limit visibility, it is probably worth finding another space.” Do you have any other parking tips for drivers? Let us know in the comments.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A cafe in Cambridgeshire has been described by visitors as "a great addition to the village" with the "best breakfast ever". Little Piggy, in Fenstanton, currently sits at the top of Tripadvisor's list of cafés in the county, boasting a 4.9-star rating from more than 130 customer reviews. The café on High Street has become a favourite among diners, with customers regularly praising its friendly service, generous portions and welcoming atmosphere. Reviewers have singled out the quality of the food, describing meals as delicious, well-presented and good value for money. The café's décor and inviting setting were also frequently mentioned in customer feedback. One review said: "I have been to this cafe a couple of times now. The staff are friendly and the food is always nice. It is also a big bonus when you have a dog being groomed across the road at fairy dog mother. I will be back." Another enthusiastically declared their experience as the "best breakfast ever!!!!!!!!!", adding: "The food was very very good. I absolutely loved all of it". A post shared by Little Piggy (@littlepiggyfenstanton) Little Piggy offers a range of breakfast, brunch and lunch dishes, including its popular Pig Out Brekkie, Signature Hash and Smashed Avocado on Toast. The family-run business was also awarded Tripadvisor's Travellers' Choice 2025 accolade, an award given to businesses that consistently receive positive reviews from travellers. Located at 21 High Street in Fenstanton, the café is open from Wednesday to Saturday, with Sunday opening hours from 9.30am until 3pm. One reviewer described the café as offering "excellent" food and service, while others praised the homemade cakes, relaxed atmosphere and welcoming team. Tripadvisor says customers frequently comment on the restaurant's reasonable prices and high-quality meals. The ranking places Little Piggy ahead of other highly-rated Cambridgeshire cafés, including Marmalade & Jam in Ely and Fontanella's in Whittlesey. Have you visited Little Piggy? summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Urgent repairs needed at historic church threatened by water damage
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A council has agreed to help fund “urgent repairs” to a village church amid safety concerns. St Andrew’s Church in Wimpole had already spent £14,000 of their own money repairing the aging building from damage caused by water ingress and deteriorating masonry. The Grade II listed building is owned by the Diocese of Ely and, as well as providing church services, also hosts concerts, community events and art exhibitions. But the church’s future has been put at risk with water damage causing staining, plaster deterioration and even falling debris. The church applied for £2,000 of funding from South Cambridgeshire District Council’s community chest to continue repairs. This will also go towards restoring two historic monuments – reattaching the lion to the effigy of Thomas Chicheley and cleaning and refixing the brass plaque to Reginald York. The Church Is Located On The Wimpole Estate. Credit: Google Maps This will cost £3,719 while the roof and masonry work will cost £11,234. The church said they will meet their remaining costs through fundraising activities, existing reserves, private donations and applications to external funders. They have submitted applications to the Cambridge Historic Churches Trust and the Heritage Lottery Fund – and secured a £1,000 private donation, with indications of future private support. Council officers recommended approving the funding as it would support “the continued use of a well-used community facility and heritage site, ensuring it remains accessible to residents, visitors and researchers for years to come”. They said the repairs were necessary to stop the building deteriorating further and to improve public safety. The council approved the funding.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: RSPCA Block Fen: 'Gentle giant' Mastiff looking for a home
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: For RSPCA Block Fen's latest 'Find Me a Home' appeal, Lloyd asks: "Can you give me a home?" Mastiff Lloyd is a staff favourite at RSPCA Block Fen in Cambridgeshire and has a sweet, affectionate and loyal nature. Being only one, he still has a lot to learn about the world around him - but with the right owner, staff think he would thrive. A spokesperson for the centre said: “Lloyd really is a gentle giant and we all adore him. It’s heartbreaking that he hasn’t had the easiest start in his short life. But since coming to the centre, he is growing in confidence every day and his wonderful personality is really shining through. “Like many young dogs, Lloyd is still learning about the world around him. Since arriving with us, he has made fantastic progress and is becoming increasingly relaxed with new people, especially when introductions are calm and at his own pace. Once he gets to know you, Lloyd's affectionate and loyal nature really shines through. “Our gorgeous boy is looking for an adult-only home where he can enjoy a predictable routine and continue building his confidence. A quieter home in a rural or semi-rural setting, with peaceful walking routes and fewer day-to-day distractions, would suit him perfectly and help him continue making positive strides. “He would be best as the only pet in the home. While he enjoys seeing other dogs from a comfortable distance, he can sometimes find close encounters a little overwhelming. Being the centre of someone's world will allow him to keep developing his confidence and create a strong bond with his new family. “Lloyd has so much potential and is ready for the next chapter of his life. With patient, understanding adopters, plenty of encouragement, and a calm environment, we're confident he'll continue to blossom into the devoted, loving companion we already know he is.” Experience with large or Mastiff-type breeds would be an advantage, as Lloyd is a big, strong lad. Despite his size, he has made lovely progress with his lead walking and enjoys getting out and exploring. He's becoming more settled on walks and is continuing to learn that the world isn't such a scary place. If you think you might match our criteria for rehoming an animal, please complete our Online Application Form. Figures released as part of the RSPCA’s Cruelty Hurts, Love Rescues fundraising campaign show cruelty reports peak over the summer; and that summer cruelty is the worst it’s been. Last summer, the charity received 6,322 cruelty calls to their emergency line - or one call every 10 minutes (when the line is open). That’s a shocking 64% increase over the last five years. Personality I'd prefer an adult-only household. I'm a shy guy; I'll need time to settle. I need to learn how to play.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: High street chain hosts closing down sale with £1 items in major restructuring plan
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A popular stationery shop chain has launched a closing-down sale with customers able to get some final bargains as prices start from just £1. TG Jones, formerly known as WH Smith, has secured court approval for a major restructuring, which is expected to lead to the closure of around 150 stores and affect hundreds of jobs. In July, TG Jones’ restructuring plan was approved by the High Court in a move which will save the business from insolvency. Closing-down sale signs have appeared in TG Jones shops across the UK, with customers also able to shop its sale online. TG Jones’ website is giving customers the chance to buy items for as little as £1, with everything from gift bags to books and toys included in the closing-down sale. The retailer warned online customers: “Don't miss your last chance to buy and grab your favourites for less today - once items in our Sale are gone, they really are gone forever!” Online offers include: It has been announced that stores in Essex (Basildon, Southend and Maldon) will close in September and October, and the Stroud store is also hosting a sale for customers before it leaves the high street. The chain of shops was renamed to TG Jones last year after being bought by Modella, while WH Smith kept its group of stores in travel locations such as airports and train stations. A post shared by TGJones (@tgjonesuk) There are around 450 TG Jones stores with 4,700 staff, mostly in the UK. It previously warned that the overhaul would put jobs at risk, but didn’t disclose how many workers will be affected. In July, Alex Willson, chief executive of TG Jones, said: “We welcome the court’s approval of our restructuring plan. “This decision allows us to move ahead with our turnaround strategy. “The plan protects the substantial core of the store estate and makes TG Jones a stronger, more sustainable business. “We are incredibly grateful to all the colleagues, partners and stakeholders who engaged constructively throughout the process, and to Modella Capital for its continued financial commitment.” Recommended reading: Tom Smith KC, for TG Jones, said that the “working assumption” is that around 150 stores will close as a result of the plans, as landlords who do not wish to accept the reduced rate can choose to terminate the lease. He also said the company has suffered from “long-term sales decline”, exacerbated by high inflation, increased online shopping, reduced consumer spending, with higher labour costs and taxes. The rebranding from WH Smith has also damaged sales, he added. Is your local TG Jones store closing its doors? Let us know in the comments.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Unpaid carers invited to help shape future support services
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Unpaid carers in Cambridgeshire are being invited to help shape the future of support services. Cambridgeshire County Council is gathering insights from carers and those with lived experience of caring to help design future adult carer support services in the county. A series of workshops will be held between September 2026 and March 2027, offering carers a chance to influence service priorities, delivery models, and commissioning plans. Graham Wilson, chair of the council’s Adults and Health Committee, said: "Unpaid carers play a vital role in supporting loved ones and helping people live independently. "Their contribution is often unseen, but makes a huge difference to individuals, families and communities across Cambridgeshire. "We are committed to enabling full and healthy lives for all residents by helping to build strong community ties and supporting independent living. "That means listening to the people who use and rely on our services. "Carers understand better than anyone the challenges and opportunities that come with caring responsibilities, and their experiences are invaluable in helping us shape future support. "This is an opportunity for carers to have a real say in how services are developed. "I would encourage anyone with experience of caring to get involved and help us ensure support meets the needs of carers now and in the future." The first workshop will take place on Friday, September 18, from 10.30am to 12.30pm at Huntingdon Library. Attendees will discuss what future carer services should prioritise and the outcomes they want to see. This work also supports The Big Conversation on Care, which launched on 29 July and is the largest public conversation about adult social care in a generation. To take part or request more information, email Commissioning.FPTeam@cambridgeshire.gov.uk.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: World record attempt to test 100 men for prostate cancer in one day
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Eaton Socon Health Centre in St Neots will host an attempt to set a new world record on Saturday September 5. At least 100 men are expected to receive free prostate cancer tests and examinations in a single day. Miss Jyoti Shah MBE, a surgeon at North West Anglia NHS Foundation Trust, said: "Prostate cancer is a silent killer, but it is a cancer that we can cure if we pick it up early enough. "It is the most common cancer in men in the UK, with one in eight being diagnosed as some point in their lives – and for men from an Afro-Caribbean heritage, the risk is one in four. "I am so very proud of and thankful to my team for their dedication and giving their time to support this important community event – and to our Hospitals' Charity for meeting the cost of the PSA tests." The event is supported by the St Neots Prostate Cancer Support Group and Purple Horizons, a community interest company based in St Neots. The current registered GuinnessWorld Records for men signing up for testing in eight hours is 258 in Egypt in 2024. Each PSA blood test costs around £3.50, with funding provided by the North West Anglia Hospitals’ Charity. Miss Shah and her team will register each patient on the hospital system, review medical histories, and carry out blood tests and physical examinations. All services are offered free of charge and on a voluntary basis. Patients will receive their results directly, and their GPs will also be notified. Further follow-up information will be provided as needed. The event aims to raise awareness of prostate cancer and encourage more men to get tested.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Huntingdon martial arts club to host special seminar with leader
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A martial arts club is set to host a special self-defence seminar with a highly experienced instructor. Inspired Martial Arts in Huntingdon will welcome Stephen Sweetlove MBE to its dojo on Sunday September 20 at 10am. The event will be a unique opportunity for participants aged 16 and over to learn self-defence principles based on more than 50 years of martial arts experience. The seminar is not just about learning new skills; it's also about raising funds for the Sweetlove Cancer Nurse, a cause that will benefit from every penny raised during the event. Martial arts seminar raises funds for cancer nursing support (Image: Inspired Martial Arts) Stephen Sweetlove is a martial arts expert with several high-level grades, including 6th Dan Judo, 6th Dan Ju-Jitsu, and 5th Dan Taiho Jutsu. He is also a Master of Sport in Sambo and a recipient of the Kurash Golden Medal of Honour. The seminar will cover various aspects of personal protection. Participants will learn about Defendu, a practical self-defence system developed in the 1920s known for its application in real-world encounters. Sweetlove will also introduce concepts from Tony Blauer’s SPEAR System, which focuses on using the body’s instinctive response to sudden danger. The seminar will also cover Cooper’s Colour Code of Awareness, a straightforward framework for understanding situational awareness. The session will not be limited to experienced martial artists. Anyone aged 16 or over with an interest in personal safety is welcome to join. This inclusive approach reflects the philosophy of Inspired Martial Arts, which emphasises the importance of confidence, discipline, and awareness in effective self-defence. Self-defence expert leads charity seminar in Huntingdon (Image: Inspired Martial Arts) The seminar offers a chance for participants to gain practical self-defence knowledge while supporting a good cause. Tickets for the event are priced at £15 per person. The seminar will be held at Inspired Martial Arts Huntingdon, 10 Stonehill, Stukeley Meadows Industrial Estate, Huntingdon, PE29 6ED. For more information, contact neal@inspiredmartialarts.co.uk.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Amazing former Addenbrooke's Hospital patient Grace wins The Piano TV show
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A former Addenbrooke’s Hospital patient who lost her fingers and lower legs after contracting meningitis as a child has won Channel 4’s The Piano. Grace Matthews, 19, received a standing ovation after performing in the show’s final at Birmingham’s Symphony Hall. Pop singer Mika named her the winner after telling the audience that one performer had been able to “take the collective consciousness of thousands of strangers” and suspend it “in mid-air” through music. Grace, from Norfolk, said after hearing her name announced: “I’m shaking. I don’t know what to say. That’s insane. I did not think that would be the outcome at all, but thank you all, all, so much for coming and watching and thank you to the best contestants and partners I could ask for!” Grace Matthews, aged three (Image: CUH) Grace was three when she developed a temperature in January 2011 and was taken to Norfolk and Norwich University Hospital before being transferred to Addenbrooke’s in Cambridge. Tests confirmed meningitis and meningococcal septicaemia. She spent nine days in intensive care and became critically ill, with surgery ultimately necessary to save her life. She lost all her fingers and both lower legs. Now using prosthetic legs, Grace plays the piano using her palm, half a thumb and the stub of a little finger. Her repertoire includes music by Pink, Adele, Queen and Bruce Springsteen, and she arranges the music herself. Her mother, Vicky Matthews, said the family were “completely overwhelmed and incredibly proud”. She added: “To see how far she has come is something we will never take for granted. “We will always be grateful to the incredible team at Norfolk and Norwich University Hospitals Foundation Trust and Addenbrooke’s who saved her life.” During Grace’s recovery, her former Addenbrooke’s music therapist Dawn Loombe and hospital play specialists became a central part of her day. Grace Matthews and her former Addenbrooke’s music therapist Dawn Loombe. (Image: CUH) Despite bandages on her hands, Grace enjoyed playing eight-octave rainbow bells while Ms Loombe played the accordion or guitar. After returning home to her parents, Vicky and Brian, and brother Tom, she progressed from a small electric keyboard to a full-sized electric piano. Ms Loombe supported Grace’s application for The Piano, and the teenager first appeared in the programme in June, performing Ludovico Einaudi’s contemporary classical piece Experience. Ms Loombe, now working part-time for Suffolk Music Therapy Services after retiring from Addenbrooke’s, said: “From the first time I met Grace, it was obvious that she was incredibly resilient and musically gifted. “She loved all the instruments, particularly the accordion, guitar, piano keyboard and the rainbow bells. She wanted to play everything and could copy melodies in no time.” Grace was selected for the final after performing in front of travellers at Birmingham New Street Station during filming for the series. Her winning performance at Symphony Hall moved the 2,000-strong audience, with viewers watching her receive the show’s top prize. You can listen to her music on Spotify.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Shocking figures reveal scale of animal beatings in Cambridgeshire
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Shocking new figures have revealed a huge spike in the number of animal beatings recorded in Cambridgeshire. Data released by the RSPCA shows 276 beatings were recorded last year alone, an increase of 61 per cent compared to 2021. The animal welfare charity revealed it receives a beating report every 15 minutes which represent a staggering 85 per cent of all its animal cruelty complaints. "It’s incredibly distressing to see such a massive rise in reports of intentional beatings with one report coming to our cruelty line every 15 minutes," RSPCA superintendent Jo Hirst said. "These are often upsetting cases where animals - usually pet cats and dogs - have experienced deliberate and horrific violence - leaving animals with not only physical injuries but mental scars as well." Nationally, the RSPCA received 16,033 reports of animal beats last year - almost double since 2021, when the figure stood at 8,459. Dogs and cats usually face the brunt of these attacks, but other animals are often victims too. And according to the charity, it is often someone in the pet’s own family perpetrating the violence. "To help rescue animals from these situations we rely on the public to be our eyes and ears and report any concerns about animal abuse to us and we are grateful that so many people do and are more aware of the problem,” Hirst added. "We’re also finding that CCTV footage, doorbell cameras and smartphones are providing a view into society that we never had before, meaning that animal beatings are more likely to be caught on camera in supermarket car parks, on streets, in lifts, and even behind closed doors in the home. "This could also account for the rise that we are seeing as they are more likely to be caught on camera, uploaded to social media or reported to us." Have you got a story you want to share? summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Citizens Advice Rural Cambs gives tips on how to deal with your debts
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Meghan Hawthorne, debt caseworker at Citizens Advice Rural Cambs, talks about how debt and money problems in general can feel extremely overwhelming It is important to remember that you do not have to face this alone and we are there to support you. The biggest step forward is reaching out and asking for help. We know how nerve-wracking this can be, so in the case that you want to try and work things out yourself, or gather the relevant information before asking for debt advice, I wanted to give you some self-help tips on how to do this: Building your Budget: Knowing how much you have coming in and how much you have going out will show you how much money you have left over at the end of the month. · Start to gather bank statements, wage slips, benefit letters/information, etc. · You can build a budget sheet on paper, online or through a budgeting app. One we recommend is the online Money Helper Budget Planner: https://www.moneyhelper.org.uk/en/everyday-money/budgeting/budget-planner Collecting Information on Your Debts: Knowing exactly what you owe to whom will show you your debt total and show you who you need to be contacting about your debts. · Gather statements, bills, contracts, letters, etc. Getting your credit reports (TransUnion, Experian and Equifax) will show you what money you have borrowed, paid back and owe. · Details to collect: o Who the creditor is (who you owe money to); o How much you owe; o What stage the debt is at (when did you miss the first payment and what has the creditor done to get the money back); o Your account/reference number. Contacting Creditors: It can be a good idea to contact your creditors, explain that you are trying to deal with the debt and ask them to: · Confirm the details of the debts. · Put a pause on chasing you until you have all your information gathered and work out what you need to do. · Stop adding interest and charges, which increase the debt. IMPORTANT: If you believe your debt(s) have surpassed the limitation period (6 years), please contact us before contacting your creditors. Priority and Non-Priority Debts: Priority debts have more serious consequences and can cause particularly serious problems if you do not do anything about them. · Priority Debts can include: rent and mortgage (or secured loan) arrears, council tax arrears, energy arrears, TV licence, court fines, etc. · Non-Priority Debts can include: credit cards, catalogues, unsecured (including payday) loans, unpaid water bills, money borrowed from family and friends, etc. When to Ask for Help: · If you are struggling to deal with your priority debts and/or you have more than one priority debt and don’t know which one to deal with first; · If you have completed your budget and don’t have money left over at the end of the month; · If you want to have a look at ways of potentially increasing your income and reducing your expenditure; · You have received court paperwork and/or have been contacted/visited by bailiffs. If you decide that you need to contact us for further support, our advisers will always be happy to help and guide you in taking the relevant next steps. You can contact us on Freephone 0808 278 7807: 9.30am-3.30pm Monday, Thursday, and Friday, and from 9.30am-7pm Tuesday and Wednesday, or head to our website https://www.citizensadviceruralcambs.org.uk/ for more information.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Summer fitness tips to make exercise fun for the whole family
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Liam Rushmer, director of Cambridgeshire-based Fitness Rush Group, writes the first edition of his monthly fitness column Summer is a perfect reminder that exercise doesn't have to mean spending hours in a gym. Warmer weather naturally encourages us to venture outdoors, making it easier to move more without even realising it. With temperatures rising, it's important to train smarter, not harder. Stay hydrated throughout the day, wear lightweight clothing and, where possible, exercise during the cooler mornings or evenings. Your body works harder in hot weather, so listen to it and don't be afraid to slow the pace. The school holidays also create fantastic opportunities to build activity into family life. A walk along the beach, exploring a country park, swimming, cycling, paddleboarding, trampoline parks or simply playing games in the garden all count towards a healthier lifestyle. The best exercise is often the activity you enjoy enough to keep doing and are more likely to continue with it. Rather than focusing on calories burned, focus on creating memories. Children don't remember how many steps they walked, but they'll remember the adventures they had. Adults are no different. Aim to move every day, even if it's just a gentle walk after dinner or a family day exploring somewhere new. Every step contributes to your physical and mental wellbeing. As summer draws to a close, routines begin to return. Next month we'll look at how to build healthy habits that fit around busy work and school schedules, making exercise something that works with your lifestyle rather than against it.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Leading Hunts councillor details where our food waste goes after collection
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A leading Huntingdonshire councillor has moved to clear up confusion surrounding the disposal of the district's food waste. Residents had raised concerns about where food waste, which is now being collected by the district council, is sent for processing, with some believing it was being taken to the Envar site in Woodhurst. The confusion followed a recent site visit by MP Ben Obese-Jecty, who toured Envar to discuss operations and potential future plans, including a proposed medical waste incinerator. Councillor Julie Kerr, the council's executive councillor for parks and countryside, waste and street scene, posted on Facebook and said: "This is a clarification about HDC food waste service: Cllr Julie Kerr, who is the council's executive councillor for waste, has posted clarification on where food waste collected in the district ends up. (Image: Submitted) "There has been a lot of discussion following the recent visit to Envar by our MP Ben Obese-Jecty and some of the information subsequently shared on Facebook about where Huntingdonshire’s household food waste goes. "I think it is important that residents have the correct information." She explained that although Envar processes the district's green bin waste, food waste collected by Huntingdonshire District Council is managed through a separate system. This waste is sent to the Alconbury waste transfer station before being transported to an anaerobic digestion facility in March. Cllr Kerr said: "It is also important not to confuse the different waste streams. Read more Hunts district council asks for feedback on weekly food waste collections Fitness chain with 467 sites across the UK eyeing up 60 more new sites in 2026 Live updates as motorcyclist seriously injured in A14 crash Ex Cambs police officer accused of 'inappropriate' relationship with woman WATCH: Hammer-wielding thief caught on camera smashing his way into Cambs jewellers "HDC’s relationship with Envar relates to garden-waste disposal. "The food waste from Huntingdonshire is deposited at Alconbury waste transfer station, then it’s sent to the March Anaerobic Digestion plant for processing under the Private Finance Initiative (PFI) Contract that Cambridgeshire County Council has." At the March facility, food waste is processed to generate renewable energy and produce nutrient-rich material for use on farmland. Plastic bags are removed from the waste before processing. Cllr Kerr also addressed common questions about caddies and liners, noting that any type of liner can be used as long as it is not made of thick plastic. She said compostable bags are ideal, but bags such as bread plastic bags are also acceptable as long as bags used are not black plastic or bags for life. She encouraged residents to refer to the Huntingdonshire District Council website for official information. She said: "I appreciate that there are now a number of questions being asked by residents, and some of those questions are not currently covered on the website. "I have therefore asked officers to update the food waste information so that the additional questions being raised by residents are answered clearly and publicly. "I will also continue to make sure that residents have access to the information they need rather than having to rely on social media posts or assumptions about what happens to their waste." A food waste collections survey is currently open and will remain available until September 3. Cllr Kerr encouraged participation, describing it as an important opportunity to provide feedback on the service. During his visit to Envar, Mr Obese-Jecty discussed site operations and the proposed medical waste incinerator, which he opposes. The MP said: "I made it clear to Envar that I am against the plans to construct a medical waste incinerator and have been vocally against it since before I even became an MP, raising it with the Secretary of State, Angela Rayner, when she granted their appeal in 2024. "My thanks to Envar for taking the time to listen to my concerns and those of residents regarding the smell of the waste recycling process and the proposed plans for the medical waste incinerator." He asked people to let him know their concerns regarding the future construction of an incinerator at the site, and the impact it may have on them. He noted that a planning application for the incinerator has not yet been submitted. Envar’s next proposed development is an anaerobic digestion facility, with the incinerator potentially to follow. The MP also addressed complaints about odours from the site, especially during recent hot weather. He said there was no excess odour during his visit, despite high temperatures at the time.

Plans for a second 3G football pitch at One Leisure St Ives have been approved by Huntingdonshire District Council, despite concerns from nearby residents over noise. The council’s development management committee voted 11 in favour, with two abstentions, to approve the proposal at its recent meeting. The decision allows for a new artificial grass pitch at the California Road leisure site, alongside an existing 3G facility. The application was before the committee as the council itself, as owner and operator of One Leisure, was the applicant. A view from the south west corner of the One Leisure site. (Image: HDC) The development includes a 97m by 61m 3G artificial grass pitch, capable of accommodating adult 11-a-side football, nine-a-side, seven-a-side and five-a-side games. It will also include: The new pitch will be built south of the existing 3G pitch, on land currently used for cricket. Two replacement non-turf cricket pitches will be provided elsewhere within the wider leisure complex before construction starts. Two objections were received raising concerns that noise from the existing pitch would be made worse by the new facility. The existing 3G pitch. (Image: HDC) Councillors questioned whether the noise assessment accounted for both artificial pitches operating at the same time. Officers confirmed that it did, and said the council’s environmental health team had not objected. The report said general noise from the new pitch was expected to fall to around 46 decibels at the nearest properties, below the World Health Organisation’s 50-decibel guideline for garden areas. Intermittent sounds, such as whistles and shouting, were modelled at up to 62 decibels at the closest homes, but officers concluded this would not cause material harm when considered alongside the site’s established sports use and proposed mitigation. A plan showing the site layout. (Image: HDC) The pitch will be restricted to use between 8am and 10pm daily. Conditions will also require a noise management plan, a complaints and investigation process, and neoprene fittings designed to reduce the sound of balls striking the fencing. The proposed LED floodlights will be designed to direct light onto the pitch. Officers said replacing heads on the existing lighting columns would reduce edge light spill in some areas from about 46m to 18m, even with the additional pitch. Ecologists identified bats using the site for foraging and commuting, including light-sensitive species. Cllr Warren Smith front right chaired the meeting. (Image: HDC) Officers said the directional lighting and landscaping proposals would mitigate potential effects, while the development is expected to provide a 10.48% biodiversity net gain entirely on site. The plans retain 186 car parking spaces and 26 cycle spaces. A worst-case weekend-morning assessment estimated that the new pitch could require 96 spaces, leaving 90 available for the wider facility. The county highways authority did not object. St Ives Town Council supported the plans, while asking for consideration of parking and California Road maintenance. Sport England also raised no objection, subject to conditions on replacement cricket provision, pitch certification and long-term management. Before permission is formally issued, officers have been delegated authority to complete a detailed assessment against the National Planning Policy Framework, which was updated on the day of the meeting, and to add any necessary conditions.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Thameslink’s notorious 'ironing-board' seats are finally being scrapped after years of complaints from uncomfortable commuters. More than 60,000 seat base cushions will be replaced with upgraded versions featuring improved backrests, promising a more comfortable journey for passengers across one of the UK’s busiest rail networks. The upgrade comes less than 100 days after Thameslink’s operator, Govia Thameslink Railway (GTR), was brought into public ownership. Heidi Alexander, transport secretary, said: "This is what public ownership looks like in action. "Less than 100 days since GTR transferred into public control, we're delivering on the improvements commuters have been asking for. "From next year, we’ll start getting rid of the dreaded ‘ironing board seats’ so passengers can enjoy comfier, more pleasant journeys on some of Britain's busiest commuter routes." First class seating will retain its current backrest design but will also receive improved seat base cushions. Seat back tables will be added to the 70 trains that do not currently have them. Transport secretary Heidi Alexander. (Image: Laurie Noble/UK Parliament/PA Wire) GTR says the upgrades will be rolled out over two years from next year, following extensive customer testing. Ms Alexander added: "We know fixing Britain's railway is more than a refurb job and moves like this are just the start of putting our railway back on the right track. "We've frozen fares for the first time in 30 years and publicly owned operators have added 76,000 extra seats on to the network. "Once established, Great British Railways will focus relentlessly on delivering a reliable, modern service that puts passenger experience at the heart of everything it does." This is one of several improvements planned by GTR following its move into public ownership in May 2026. Other changes include increased Gatwick Express services in December and an ongoing fleet-wide refresh of toilet facilities to remove graffiti. John Whitehurst, CEO at GTR, said: "Our customers tell us that comfort matters, which is why we've been working on plans to improve seating on Thameslink services and give the millions of people who use our extensive network a better experience. "Through customer research with everyday commuters, we've gathered valuable insight to help us shape the best possible solution for cushion comfort onboard our high-capacity trains. "We're pleased to move forward with plans and bring about those much-expected improvements."

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Cambs hospital staff shortlisted for award after dramatic car park birth
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Two Cambridgeshire hospital staff have been shortlisted for an "outstanding achievement" award after they helped during a dramatic car park birth. The incident took place at Hinchingbrooke Hospital in the early hours of Easter Saturday, when Katie Good and her partner James Gingell from Peterborough arrived at the hospital as advised by the maternity team. However, before Katie could even make it across the car park, baby Oliver arrived unexpectedly. James said: "What followed happened incredibly quickly. "During the next contraction, Katie was standing holding on to me when her waters broke and in that same moment, our baby was born – so suddenly that he arrived into her clothing before we had fully grasped what was happening." Healthcare assistant Sam Craigie and interim deputy divisional nursing director Ana Jardim were nearby and rushed to help. Sam and Ana were nominated for an award for their quick thinking (Image: North West Anglia NHS Foundation Trust) Ana said: "When we arrived, things were moving very quickly and we had time to support the baby's head and helped mum onto the floor. "Both mum and dad were very emotional, and we were able to tell them it was a boy." The pair supported Katie safely to the ground and gently retrieved baby Oliver from her clothing, placing him on her chest in the moments before Emergency Department and Labour Ward staff arrived. Sam even took off his uniform to wrap baby Oliver in. The quick-acting duo were shortlisted in the Health Hero category at North West Anglia NHS Foundation Trust's Outstanding Achievement Awards. The five were reunited at the ceremony, held at Peterborough Cathedral. Katie said: "It meant so much to us to meet the incredible people who helped us when Oliver made his surprise arrival in the hospital car park. Baby Oliver arrived before his mum Katie could even make it across the car park (Image: North West Anglia NHS Foundation Trust) "We've thought about them so often over the last few months, so having the opportunity to thank them in person was incredibly emotional and something we'll never forget. "It was also lovely to see their reaction to meeting Oliver all these months later – it really brought everything full circle. "It is a story we will tell for the rest of our lives, and one in which Trust staff will always be remembered with deep gratitude." James echoed her sentiments. He said: "In what could have been a moment of panic, Sam and Ana's composure and kindness brought an immediate sense of safety. “We are immensely grateful to every single person involved - from those who came running to help, to those who continued our care inside the hospital - in what was an unforgettable and dramatic start to Easter Saturday.”
