summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Cambridgeshire man who harassed ex-partner and left her 'living in fear' jailed
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A Cambridgeshire man who harassed his ex-partner and left her "living in fear" has been jailed. Ashley Smith, 38, of Eastleigh Road in Eastfield, Peterborough, was sentenced to two years behind bars on August 20 at Cambridge Crown Court after admitting to three counts of harassment in breach of a restraining order. The order had been issued on May 5 after Smith was convicted of stalking his former partner. Less than a month after the order was imposed, the victim discovered multiple missed calls from a withheld number, which she believed to be from Smith. He called again later that day and contacted a friend of the victim, who recorded the conversation. In the call, Smith asked about the victim’s whereabouts and whether she was with another man. He said that if she had a boyfriend, he would "kill him." Smith went on to make 22 more calls that afternoon, all of which were ignored, and the following month he continued to contact her from a withheld number. When she eventually answered, Smith threatened to come to her home and demanded to know who she was with. Ashley Smith admitted three counts of harassment in breach of a restraining order (Image: Cambridgeshire Police) He told her she had "ruined his life" and threatened that she "wasn’t going to get away with it." In a call the next day, Smith said: "You're dead tomorrow, you'll die. "I swear on my mother's life you're dead." Detective Constable Kyle Miskin, who investigated the case, said: "Smith’s behaviour left the victim living in fear and constantly looking over her shoulder. "Despite being made subject to a restraining order, he repeatedly ignored the conditions and continued to contact and threaten her." Smith was arrested at Stansted Airport on June 18. DC Miskin said: "Everyone has the right to feel safe following the end of a relationship. "Stalking, harassment and controlling behaviour can have a devastating impact on victims, and we will always take reports seriously and do everything we can to protect those affected. "I hope this sentence provides the victim with some reassurance and allows her to move forward with her life."

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: National Trust estate faces shortage of hay due to drought conditions
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A Cambridgeshire National Trust estate is facing a hay shortage as grass growth has stalled in drought conditions, with livestock forced on to winter feed months early. Hay meadows that normally produce 150 tonnes at Wimpole Estate in Cambridgeshire have yielded nothing, the conservation charity said. It is the third time in five years the estate has faced severe drought impacts and in response conservationists are accelerating a programme of climate adaptation. This includes tree planting, work to increase rainwater storage, and conservation grazing to reduce wildfire risk and support habitat restoration. The National Trust said selective breeding is also helping livestock cope better with dry conditions. Livestock have been forced onto winter feed months early (Image: The National Trust/PA Wire) Dave Hassall, National Trust farm and countryside manager, said: “Drought affects every part of the system – crops, grassland, livestock, wildlife and costs. “We’re already using winter feed because summer growth simply hasn’t happened. “These pressures are being felt across all farming systems, and they show why adapting to a changing climate is essential for food production, nature and rural communities.” Parkland affected by drought at Wimpole Estate in Cambridgeshire (Image: The National Trust/PA Wire) The National Trust said Wimpole Estate is its largest organic in‑hand farm, with 1,200 hectares (3,000 acres) of land. Grain yields are down by around 25%, and straw production has fallen from 200 bales to just 60. Wildlife habitats are under pressure, with invasive species such as ragwort and thistles spreading rapidly in the dry conditions, and soil health has suffered with cracked ground. Veteran trees are showing signs of stress, and disrupted weather patterns are creating mismatches between flowering plants and pollinating insects – with consequences for both biodiversity and food production. It is the third time in five years that the estate has faced severe drought impacts (Image: The National Trust/PA Wire) Efforts are under way to help the estate adapt in the face of climate change, with 125,000 trees planted since 2021 to improve shade, soil health, moisture retention and habitat resilience. The estate is trialling alternative forage sources such as willow and aspen, and exploring more drought-tolerant crop varieties. Mr Hassall said Wimpole Estate “has adapted for 2,000 years” and “that spirit continues”. In response, conservationists are accelerating a programme of climate adaptation (Image: The National Trust/PA Wire) He added: “We welcome recent Government support for farmers, but long‑term resilience requires sustained investment in nature and climate adaptation. “We cannot do this alone.” The National Trust is calling on the Government to make climate resilience a national mission, led at Cabinet level, to invest in nature as essential infrastructure, and to support fire and rescue services. Members of the public can back this call by signing the trust’s petition at nationaltrust.org.uk/wildfire-petition.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Hunts girl, eight, to swim five miles for terminally ill great grandma
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: An eight year old girl from Huntingdonshire is set to swim five miles to raise money for her terminally ill great grandma. Isla, from Hartford near Huntingdon, is raising money for Brain Tumour Research by swimming five miles in honour of her much loved Great Nanny, who has been diagnosed with terminal glioblastoma. Glioblastoma are grade 4 brain tumours which are aggressive and often treated through chemotherapy, radiation therapy and surgery. The original challenge began as a two-mile swim, but Isla reached her £500 fundraising target so quickly that it was increased to £1,000. Isla's great grandma has been diagnosed with terminal glioblastoma (Image: Supplied) Encouraged by the response, Isla decided to increase her swim to five miles – the equivalent of around 322 lengths of a 25-metre pool. She will complete the challenge over several 500 metre sessions, aiming to complete the full five miles by September 26. Isla said: "I want to make Great Nanny proud and show her that even though I’m only eight, I can do something big for someone I love." As of August 23, Isla has completed 87 lengths, the equivalent to 1.35 miles. According to Isla's proud mum Freya, she has had amazing support from her family members who are cheering her on as she completes the swim. Isla’s fundraiser has already raised more than £800 and donations can be made through her JustGiving page. Isla is aiming to complete the full five miles by September 26 (Image: Francelli Photography) Her grandparents said they hope Isla’s story will inspire further support for Brain Tumour Research and raise awareness about brain tumours. They said: "We are incredibly proud of our granddaughter and her determination to do something so special for someone she loves." Brain tumours can affect anyone at any age and each year, nearly 13,000 people are diagnosed with a brain tumour. For more information, visit the Brain Tumour Research website.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Huntingdon Boat Club celebrates wins at Peterborough Weekend Regatta
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Huntingdon Boat Club enjoyed a successful weekend at the Peterborough Weekend Regatta on August 15 and 16, securing victories across the two days of racing. Saturday got off to an excellent start for HBC, with Hetty Weston-Leech taking victory in the Women’s Junior 14 single sculls. Weston-Leech won her heat to qualify for the final, where she produced an extremely close finish against Globe Rowing Club. Daniel & Edward (Image: Supplied) She crossed the line first in 4:52.3, just one tenth of a second ahead of Globe’s crew, who finished in 4:52.4. He then doubled up with Daniel Grant in the Open Double Sculls, narrowly missing out on another win to Peterborough Rowing Club. Grant also reached the final of the Open Single Sculls. Jasmine Yallop and Hetty Weston-Leech won their heat in the Women’s Junior 15 Double Sculls before finishing third in the final. summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Town ‘kept in dark’ over controversial car park plans
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Find, save and share Public Notices that affect you in the  area. The Public Notice Portal carries statutory public notices published in local newspapers and is the fastest and most effective way of finding out what is happening in YOUR neighbourhood. A town council has accused a developer of leaving them in the dark over controversial proposals to build on a bus station and car park. Capital and Centric has proposed to turn Huntingdon bus station and Princes Street car park into 78 new homes and a “centralised hub” for businesses with green spaces. They have released similar proposals for St Neots and St Ives, sparking controversy across Huntingdonshire. Huntingdonshire District Council’s Liberal Democrat-led coalition even collapsed over the plans when two Green councillors left due to the council’s handling of the proposals. A special meeting of Huntingdon Town Council’s planning committee was held on Tuesday August 25 after the developer held their first public consultations last week and residents shared their concerns. Pam Hunt said she thought the plans were “unacceptable” and Princes Street car park is very “well used”. Peter Snow said: “Capital and Centric are trying to propose taking things away from the community but I don’t see what they are trying to give back – that’s why they are getting a lot of bad feelings.” He asked how much research the firm had done to suggest taking away a “well-used” car park. Angela Makey, owner of Niche Comic Book Shop, raised concerns over the impact of the loss of so many parking spaces. She said: “At the moment we’re a very short walk from Princes Street car park and losing a lot of those parking spaces will have a huge impact, not just on us. “We have a sustainable model because we’ve been going for such a long time, no new business will have that level of loyalty.” Guy Makey said that a lot of acts use the car park for carrying equipment to the Commemoration Hall and, without it, they could “simply move to a different venue”. He said: “As mentioned earlier, we lost Shakespeare at the George – which was very much the jewel in the crown of Huntingdon. It would be heart-breaking if the same happened to the Commemoration Hall.” Concerns were also raised about the proposal’s impact on the Cromwell Museum – both for those driving and those travelling by bus. Councillor David Landon Cole, chair of the planning committee, said: “I wish it was in our power to make a decision on this – it isn’t – but we do hear you.” The town council can only advise on planning applications, which are decided at the district level. A formal application to the district council has not yet been made. Cllr Phil Pearce said it was an “absolute disgrace” they were not made aware of the plans while six members of Huntingdonshire District Council sat on the town council. He said: “We hear your objections, we have the same concerns as yourself – we have been kept in the dark as much as you have. “There are other sites in Huntingdon which haven’t been considered and I think us as taxpayers really ought to be asking for our money back. “We’ve been let down – we’ve been kept in the dark and treated like mushrooms.” Cllr Alan Brugnoli said that during the consultation in Market Square the developer said it was “just a proposal – something ethereal”. He said: “They have been given this money and produced nothing at the minute. “They want high end properties with what they consider no parking, I just disagree. “Anyone that can afford to commute to London and back again, first is not spending money in the local community, but also they are going to have a car.” Cllr Pearce said that the bus station plans did not have enough bus stops to replace those lost which shows “an absolute lack of research”. Questions were raised around the three bus stops proposed to replace the station, which currently has 10 bays, and the lack of consultation with bus operators. Cllr Landon Cole said: “I don’t understand how you can design a bus station without talking to the bus operator, it’s very weird.” Cllr Pearce said: “I think Capital and Centric have lost the trust of the public and it’s going to take a lot to get that back.” Cllr Landon Cole said: “The lack of communication between Capital and Centric, HDC and the public is a real problem. “We [Huntingdon Town Council] hope this doesn’t damage support for redevelopment, but understand if it has. “If Capital and Centric are to remain in Huntingdon, they have a lot of work to do to rebuild trust – they didn’t offer anything to the people of Huntingdon, but tried to take things away.” The council agreed to co-sign a letter with the Commemoration Hall objecting to the plans, agreeing with one already submitted by the Cromwell Museum.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Five-year-old Hunts girl 'lucky' to be alive after appointment spots tumour
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A five-year-old girl from St Neots was diagnosed with a brain tumour just 12 hours after an eye test led to an urgent referral to hospital. Phoebe Carpenter had been suffering from sickness and severe headaches for several months before her mother, Katie Nicholls, arranged an appointment at Specsavers in May. The optician contacted the family after the test and advised them to go straight to Addenbrooke’s Hospital in Cambridge. A CT scan later revealed that Phoebe had a brain tumour. Phoebe Carpenter pictured on her way to the operating theatre for surgery to remove a brain tumour. (Image: Carpenter family) Katie, 41, said: “On our way home from the appointment, the optician called to say that, after speaking to his senior, we should go straight to A and E at Addenbrooke’s Hospital. “I felt like we were probably wasting the hospital’s time because Phoebe was running around playing like normal but, looking back, she was probably the sickest kid there.” Phoebe had previously been taken to a GP after months of symptoms. Katie said she was told her daughter may have migraines and was asked to keep a symptoms diary. After doctors carried out the CT scan, they told the family that Phoebe had a brain tumour. Phoebe Carpenter and her family pictured at Disneyland. (Image: Carpenter family) Katie said: “I fell apart and just sobbed and sobbed. I kept thinking, how am I going to tell her dad and the other children? “I kept asking if Phoebe would survive, but the doctors said they were unable to answer that at that time, which is the worst thing in the world as a parent.” Phoebe had a drain inserted to relieve pressure on her brain caused by hydrocephalus, a build-up of cerebrospinal fluid. The following day, she underwent a 10-hour operation in which surgeons removed most of the tumour. Phoebe Carpenter pictured after undergoing major brain surgery after being diagnosed with a tumour. (Image: Carpenter family) It was later confirmed as a pilocytic astrocytoma - a slow-growing brain tumour that usually affects children. Phoebe returned to school just three weeks after the operation, initially attending for a few hours before building up to full days. By the end of term, she had completed a full week. Katie said: “Phoebe is amazing. She went back to school three weeks after her operation. “She now wears glasses which are mega strong, but she’s very comfortable wearing them.” Phoebe Carpenter was left with a large scar after her operation. (Image: Carpenter family) Phoebe does not currently need chemotherapy or radiotherapy and remains under surveillance. Her first follow-up MRI scan is scheduled for November. Katie said: “Being told Phoebe had a brain tumour was the worst feeling in the world, but now we just feel so incredibly lucky because it could have been a whole different story. “If it’s just that she now has bad eyesight and wears glasses, then so be it. We are hopeful that this is the end of it, but we have seen just how quickly your life can change.” Katie completed Brain Tumour Research’s 88 Squats in July challenge to raise money and awareness after Phoebe’s treatment. Phoebe Carpenter pictured after her surgery and on the mend. (Image: Carpenter family) She said: “I just felt like I needed to do something to give back after the amazing care Phoebe received. We just feel so lucky. “Funding for research into brain tumours is so important because this really could happen to anyone. You never think something like this will happen to you, but it does.” Brain Tumour Research says brain tumours kill more children and adults under 40 than any other cancer, but just 1% of national cancer research spending has been allocated to the disease since records began in 2002. Phoebe Carpenter underwent major brain surgery after being diagnosed with a tumour. (Image: Carpenter family) Phoebe Carpenter underwent major brain surgery after being diagnosed with a tumour. (Image: Carpenter family) Phoebe Carpenter pictured with her older brothers. (Image: Carpenter family) Phoebe Carpenter and her family pictured at Disneyland. (Image: Carpenter family) Phoebe Carpenter and her older brothers. (Image: Carpenter family) Phoebe Carpenter was able to return to school three weeks after her brain surgery. (Image: Carpenter family) Katie completed a gym challenge to raise awareness and funding for research into brain tumours. (Image: Carpenter family) Dr Noble added: “We’re incredibly grateful to Katie for raising vital awareness by sharing Phoebe’s story. The current funding for research is insufficient to deliver new, more effective treatments. That is why we are campaigning for governments to increase the national investment in research into brain tumours to at least £45 million per year."

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Man who exposed himself to women and young girls avoids prison
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A man who deliberately exposed himself to women and young girls in Cambridgeshire and Suffolk has avoided prison. Gabriel Riclea, 21, pleaded guilty to five counts of exposure at Ipswich Magistrates' Court on Tuesday August 25. The incidents occurred between October 28 and December 12, 2025, with four in Red Lodge nd the fifth in Swaffham Bulbeck, in Cambridgeshire. Each report to police indicated that a man was deliberately exposing himself to women, including two victims aged just 15 at the time. Riclea, of Malt Close, Newmarket, was handed a two-year community order. In addition to the community order, he must be registered with the police in according with the Sexual Offences Act 2003 for five years. Riclea mst also complete a 26-day programme and undertake a 10-day rehabilitation activity requirement. Detective Constable Rebecca McHugh, who was the officer in charge of the case, said: "Riclea’s actions were repeated, deliberate and entirely unacceptable. "He exposed himself to children and to women walking or jogging alone, for his own sexual gratification. "He has offered no explanation or apologies for his behaviour, which have caused his victims and others to feel unsafe in their local communities. "I would like to thank the victims for their bravery in reporting the incidents to police, and for their support in this investigation. "If unchallenged, exposure can escalate toward more serious sexual and violent offences, and I encourage anyone who has been a victim of this type of crime to report it immediately to police." Rail replacement bus services in operation on the following routes: The work involves the final stages of testing ahead of the introduction of digital in-cab signalling, which replaces traditional lineside signals with real-time information delivered directly to train drivers. Ricky Barsby, Network Rail head of access integration for the East Coast Digital Programme, said: "The work taking place involves the final preparations for us to begin a gradual introduction of digital in-cab signalling on the East Coast Main Line. "The ability to control trains in this way will enable a more resilient and reliable railway that is fit for the future. The Met Office said: "A band of heavy showers and thunderstorms is expected to move northwards on Wednesday morning. "A drier, brighter interlude may follow, but with a chance of further showers and thunderstorms breaking out during the afternoon. "Large hail and frequent lightning are also possible. "The showers and thunderstorms will drift northwards and ease during the evening." There is a small chance of sudden flooding affecting homes and businesses, potentially causing damage from floodwater, lightning, or hail. During thunderstorms, the safest option is to seek shelter in an enclosed space such as a car, avoiding trees and other tall structures. Those in exposed or elevated areas should move to lower ground. Weather warnings may change quickly, so residents are advised to monitor updates throughout the day.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Boy, three, injured in crocodile enclosure at Cambs zoo discharged from hospital
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A three-year-old boy who was seriously injured in a Cambridgeshire zoo’s crocodile enclosure has been discharged from hospital and is settling back in at home, his family said. The child returned home “a few weeks ago” and is “happy to be home, playing with his toys, sleeping in his own bed and being a big brother”, his parents said in an update posted online. Johnsons of Old Hurst, near Huntingdon, said in a previous social media post it was “alerted to reports that a child had allegedly been thrown into one of our crocodile enclosures” on June 18. A 30-year-old man from Norfolk was arrested on suspicion of attempted murder following the incident and was later bailed as police said he was “assessed as not being fit for interview”. The suspect in the case reportedly has learning difficulties and had been on a trip with carers, and an investigation has been launched into his care. The boy sustained serious injuries after he ended up in the crocodile enclosure (Image: Newsquest) In an update shared on a GoFundMe page on Monday, the boy’s family said it was “nice to have us all back together in the comfort of our own home”. The fundraising page was set up to support the family financially and help the boy’s recovery and rehabilitation, which has raised more than £113,000 to date. “Now that we are home, our son’s rehabilitation journey continues and we can focus on ensuring our son has the best possible chance at recovery,” his parents said in an update posted on GoFundMe. “Both of us will continue to stay by our son’s side as we support him on his rehabilitation journey. “We attend the hospital frequently to find out the next steps and we work on them together as a family. The boy's family has since broken their silence on the incident (Image: Newsquest) “All of his immediate surgeries are over with for now, which means we can now focus on rehabilitation at home.” They said that the money donated so far “has supported us financially to cover immediate costs such as our bills and mortgage”, and “also allowed us to cover our loss of wages during this time”. They said they have bought and donated new toys to the paediatric intensive care unit at Addenbrooke’s Hospital in Cambridge and to the children’s play team on the ward. The boy was “very fond of the play team” and “they helped him be a little three-year-old boy by inventing new games and teaching him new ways to use his feet in play”, his parents said. The fundraiser for the toddler has raised over £100,000 (Image: Joe Giddens/PA) They said they had also donated to the Sick Children’s Trust charity, which helps support families whose children are long-term patients or in the paediatric intensive care unit. In a previous update, the family said the boy had undergone seven operations.

Mr Warren said some had spent days, and in some cases weeks, away from home while working in difficult conditions at Holme Fen. summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A man who assaulted his estranged wife and son in an "abhorrent" attack has been jailed for more than four years. Tom Brown, 46, attacked the pair during a row that erupted over the absence of instant noodles at a home in Woodditton, near Newmarket, on January 4. Despite being separated from his wife, Brown was still living at her property at the time of the incident. The argument began in the kitchen before Brown left the house, returning about 30 minutes later. He became angry with his former partner when he discovered there were no instant noodles in the home. Their son and daughter tried to intervene, and Brown went upstairs, but he came back down shortly after and the confrontation escalated. The son helped his mother leave the kitchen, but Brown followed, tackled her to the ground, and pinned her down so she could not breathe. When the son tried to intervene, Brown pushed him to the floor, grabbed him by the throat, and strangled him for several seconds. The victims managed to escape and fled to a neighbour’s house. Brown followed them, shouting outside until police arrived and arrested him. Tom Brown attacked the pair in a row that erupted over the absence of instant noodles (Image: Cambridgeshire Police) He later tried to kick an officer in the head while being taken out of a police van at Parkside Police Station. DC Jack Sillince, who investigated the case, said: "Brown’s attack on his wife and son was abhorrent and he was incredibly hostile to police who came to intervene. "We wouldn’t have managed to secure this conviction without the support of the victims, and I’d particularly like to praise the son who protected his mum. "He was given a High Sheriff’s commendation and a £250 reward." Brown, of no fixed address, pleaded guilty at the start of his trial to two counts of actual bodily harm and one count of common assault of an emergency worker. He denied two counts of intentional strangulation which will remain on file. Brown was jailed for four years and eight months at Cambridge Crown Court on August 21 and handed a 15-year restraining order against the victims.

"You don’t need a big bike, you don’t need years of experience and you don’t need to be thinking about taking an advanced test. "If you legally ride a motorcycle and would like to become a safer, smoother and more confident rider, this day is for you. "Whether somebody has recently completed their CBT and rides a 125, has returned to motorcycling after many years away, or has been riding large motorcycles for decades, there is always something more we can learn." The day concludes with a one-to-one coached ride on public roads, delivered by a nationally qualified IAM RoadSmart motorcycle Observer from PECAM. The on-road coaching is tailored to each rider’s experience and needs. The scheme is funded by The Huntingdon Freemen’s Trust with additional support from Cambridgeshire Police and PECAM’s volunteer coaches. summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: History looks at centuries of bad harvests in St Neots
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: St Neots historian Liz Davies shares a look-back on wheat harvest Bread has been a central part of our diet since the Neolithic period, over 6,000 years ago, when our hunter-gatherer ancestors began farming cereals and domesticating animals. Once people had begun to live on small farms growing cereal crops, the success of the wheat harvest, used to make bread, was of crucial importance, and across the centuries bad weather was feared because it could severely damage crops and lead to a poor harvest. A bad harvest would lead to less flour which would create bread shortages and also raise prices; and labouring families depended on bread for a large part of their diet. It was a run of poor harvests in the 1780s that sparked the French Revolution in 1789, when starving workers stormed the Bastille in Paris. The terrible weather continued into the 1790s and the failure of another harvest in 1794 led to food riots across England, including in St Neots in July 1795. By the Victorian period the successful ‘in-gathering’ of the harvest (as the St Neots Advertiser put it in 1866) was celebrated with church services, harvest suppers and local feast days. During Victorian times the Eynesbury Feast was always celebrated on the first Monday and Tuesday of September with toy and gingerbread stalls and ‘flying horses’ roundabouts on a field close to the village green. Hopefully, by the time you read this the drought of 2026, which has been the most severe drought in Britain for over 200 years, will be over. The last severe drought remembered in Britain was the drought of 1976 when locally, the hot dry weather led to hosepipe bans and water rationing and in some areas the only water available was from standpipes in the street. As the hot weather continued day after day students at Longsands School were allowed to wear their PE kit to school and the situation was so serious that the Government ran a campaign to encourage the public to use less water with its most memorable slogan being "Save water, bath with a friend". In late July the hot weather led to a plague of aphids on local farms and a company was called in to spray the crops with insecticide using a helicopter. Apart from insect problems many local farmers burnt the stubble left in their fields after the harvest and locally this started a serious fire on fields at Lower Wintringham Farm in July 1976. The fire began after a neighbouring farmer lost control of his burning stubble and set alight the unharvested wheat crop at the Wintringham farm, causing £3,000 of damage. Amazingly, the next day the same farmer himself needed the help of the fire brigade when his stubble burn again ran out of control. Drought problems continued until the end of August 1976 when Denis Howell, Minister for Sport was made the Minister for Drought but not long after that violent thunderstorms finally brought the drought to an end, although stubble burning was not banned until 1993.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Bus operator raises concerns over plans to scrap Hunts bus station
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Find, save and share Public Notices that affect you in the  area. The Public Notice Portal carries statutory public notices published in local newspapers and is the fastest and most effective way of finding out what is happening in YOUR neighbourhood. A bus operator has raised concerns over plans to redevelop a town centre and scrap the bus station. Whippet claims current proposals for Huntingdon do not include adequate facilities for bus passengers. This is espite supporting the wider scheme to deliver new homes and investment, a spokesperson said. The plans, submitted by developer Capital & Centric, would see the existing bus station and surrounding land redeveloped into a residential-led neighbourhood. Ed Cameron, managing director of Whippet, said: "We strongly support the creation of new homes in town centres, particularly where people can live within walking distance of shops, employment, leisure opportunities and sustainable transport. "Developments like this can help create thriving and sustainable communities. "What is deeply concerning, however, is that the current proposals do not include adequate provision for buses. "Operators across the region are working incredibly hard to improve services and encourage more people to travel sustainably. The car park on Princes Street in Huntingdon could be transformed into a new neighbourhood (Image: Street View) "At Whippet alone, passenger numbers have grown by over 50 per cent in the last three years, demonstrating the increasing demand for high-quality bus services. "That growth can only continue if suitable infrastructure is provided for both passengers and drivers." Under current plans, the bus station would be replaced by just three bus stops. Whippet says this is not enough to meet demand or support future growth. The station currently acts as a central interchange for passengers and an operational base for drivers. Mr Cameron said Whippet was disappointed not to have been consulted during the planning process. He said: "If Huntingdon is to encourage sustainable travel and reduce dependence on cars, public transport must be designed into developments from the outset, not treated as an afterthought. "We are keen to work constructively with Capital & Centric, Huntingdonshire District Council and other stakeholders to ensure any future redevelopment provides the facilities needed to support passengers, drivers and the continued growth of public transport in Huntingdonshire." Capital & Centric has been contacted for comment.

There is plenty for sensory-seekers to enjoy, too, especially the musical stepping stones, while a magical moment near the end is sure to stay in your little ones’ memories. Although £29 per ticket – at the cheapest price – is relatively steep, there’s no denying the charm of this adaption. Brittany Mumford, from Brampton, will descend from the world’s tallest permanent abseil tower in support of Lymphoma Action. The event, called Don’t Look Down, takes place on Saturday, September 19, during Blood Cancer Awareness Month and marks the charity’s 40th anniversary. Ms Mumford said: "When people think of cancer, they don't often picture a healthy 27-year-old mum with an eight-week-old baby in her arms – me included. "When I was sitting at the hospital during my tests, feeding my baby, I thought, 'They're making a big mistake here – I'm fine!' "Then the words 'you have cancer' brought a harsh ending to my naivety." Ms Mumford was diagnosed with Hodgkin lymphoma shortly after the birth of her second child. This September marks six years since she went into remission. She said: "Through Lymphoma Action, I found the support I really needed. "They helped me understand what I was going through and connected me with others who understood – people who knew the fear of waiting for scan results, the grief of losing your old life, the uncertainty of not knowing what comes next, and the hope of life after treatment." Ms Mumford said she hopes to raise funds and awareness for those affected by lymphoma, the most common type of blood cancer in the UK. Laura Thompson, challenge events fundraiser at Lymphoma Action, said: "We are so grateful to Brittany and her family for their support. "Our daredevil challenge would make Spiderman think twice, but every step taken down the tower by our brave abseil team will help us make sure no one faces lymphoma alone." Ms Mumford’s fundraising page can be found at justgiving.com/page/brittany-mumford-2.

Objections have been raised over plans for up to nine new homes in a Huntingdonshire village. A planning application has been submitted to Huntingdonshire District Council for permission in principle to build up to nine homes on a paddock in Brington. The application outlines the site as being west of Brington Road, though consultation documents describe it as east of The Green. The permission-in-principle process will determine if housing is suitable for the site in terms of location, use, and scale. If approved, details such as layout, design, landscaping, access, and drainage will be discussed in a later application. The planning statement argues that the proposal would "complete" an existing frontage, not extend the village into open countryside. The statement also highlights the site's proximity to the village centre, Brington Church of England Primary School, and other local amenities. However, the proposal has sparked backlash from residents. Concerns focus on the impact on Brington's character, with residents arguing that the development is not genuine infill and would alter the feel of the "beautiful small village." Flooding is another major concern, with residents fearing that new homes, hard surfaces, and the loss of permeable land could increase risks to neighbouring properties. One objection highlighted the site's open, vegetated, and "distinctly rural" nature, arguing that up to nine houses would be out of keeping with Brington’s established form. The absence of affordable housing in the proposal was also questioned. The application remains under consideration.

Police were called to Huntingdonshire District Council's offices at Pathfinder House on April 14. Matthew Howson, 33, poured a can of lighter fluid on the lobby floor and lit it with a match. He then produced a Stanley knife from his pocket, before walking out the building, leaving a member of the public to extinguish the fire. Shortly afterwards, police were called to the former Fire Station in Huntingdon, after receiving a report that a man was refusing to leave the premises. Officers recognised Howson as being responsible for the earlier incident, and arrested him after finding the Stanley knife and matches in his pocket. A bottle of lighter fluid was also found nearby. At Peterborough Crown Court on Wednesday (19 August), Howson, of Grosvenor Yard, Newmarket, was jailed for one year and ten months. He admitted to arson, possessing a knife in a public place, and breaching a stalking protection order. The final charge relates to Howson failing to notify police about a change of address. He thereby breached the order which was made by Huntingdon Magistrates Court in September 2025. DC Emily South, who investigated, said: "Howson's actions were extremely reckless and could have had serious consequences. "He deliberately started the fire inside a busy public building, putting members of the public and staff at risk. Thankfully, the fire was quickly extinguished, and nobody was injured. "This sentence reflects the danger his actions posed and how serious we treat this type of offending." Have you got a story you want to share? Get in touch at oliver.murphy@newsquest.co.uk

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A firefighter who has been tackling a wildfire at a nature reserve in Cambridgeshire for the past 12 days said he saw "huge flames" and "200 foot trees" falling around him. A blaze broke out at Holme Fen on August 8 and continues to smoulder away, burning up to six metres below the surface deep in the peat. Fire crews from across the country have been on site assisting Cambridgeshire Fire and Rescue Service. Holme Fen is a Site of Special Scientific Interest (SSSI) due to the variety of wildlife, plants and fungi found across the 657 acres of landscape. The area of destruction caused by the fire extends to 95 acres. A blaze broke out at Holme Fen on August 8 (Image: Emily Stevens) Crew Manager Jake Banks, from Merseyside Fire and Rescue Service, has been on the scene since the fire broke out. He said: "The conditions in the first seven to eight days were really, really hard. "Six to ten feet below ground, all the peat was well alight and recorded temperatures were up to 1,000 degrees." Exceptionally high temperatures and multiple heatwaves in Cambridgeshire this summer have only added to the pressure on fire crews. Crew Manager Jake Banks has been tackling the wildfire for 12 days (Image: Emily Stevens) Mr Banks said: "Obviously last week was very hot as well - 38 degrees some days here, with huge flames. "This area covers 60 football pitches in total, and then we have to battle that with all that heat and move all the hose around. "We also had the huge risk of 200 foot trees falling every couple of minutes around us, so it's been a long hard few weeks to be honest." The area of destruction covers 60 football pitches in total (Image: Emily Stevens) After nearly two weeks, there are no more open flames on site. Fire crews must now work to fell and clear out the trees in the area so they can begin to tackle the peat, which is still smouldering underground. The fire is deep in the peat, up to six metres below the surface (Image: Emily Stevens) Mr Banks said: "I think we've got a grasp on this now. "Now we're just here to support the machinery operators and make sure while they are moving all the fallen trees about, they are safe and there is no reignition anywhere." According to Assistant Chief Fire Officer Stuart Smith, it could be up to three or four weeks until the area has been cleared of trees and crews can start extinguishing the underground peat fire.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Find, save and share Public Notices that affect you in the  area. The Public Notice Portal carries statutory public notices published in local newspapers and is the fastest and most effective way of finding out what is happening in YOUR neighbourhood. Four homes have been approved at a former kennels and cattery despite fears they could “open a floodgate” of development in the countryside. Plans for five houses at the site off Fenstanton Road near Hilton had been rejected in 2022 for being out of character for the countryside and being in an unsustainable location where residents would need to drive to access services. But the latest plans for four detached four-bedroom bungalows were recommended for approval by Huntingdonshire District Council’s planning officers. A design and access statement from Twenty Nine Architecture and Planning said the new plan “significantly reduced” the scale of the homes to a “modest single-storey form” more in line with the existing buildings on the site. The former Fields View Kennels and Cattery, which shut in 2020, would be demolished to make way for the homes. Hilton Parish Council still objected to the new plans and Cllr Peter Balicki spoke on its behalf to the council’s development management committee on Monday, August 17. He said that the last proposal was originally for seven homes before being revised down to six, and finally five. He said the parish council objected to these from “concern” that if homes were approved on the former agricultural site it would “open a floodgate of applications”. He said: “It just seems that you can turn the barrel of the kaleidoscope as many times as you like until it falls into place. “Now that we’ve gone from seven failed, six failed, five failed – we’ll let permission be given for four”. James Aldridge, of nearby Alpha Farms, said he was concerned that future residents of the homes could complain about his poultry farm – despite it being there first. He said: “Our farm is already here and is a working farm – there will naturally be noise, smells, dust, farm vehicles and muck movements. “If people move into these houses and then complain about these normal farming activities, could that lead to the council putting restrictions on our farm? “We want to know that our farm can continue to operate normally in the future.” The council’s planning officer said national planning policy states that existing sites “should not have unreasonable restrictions” placed on them as a result of new developments being approved nearby. An odour assessment also took place, which was not done for the previous application, and officers said they didn’t think odour or noise would negatively impact future residents. Cllr Alan Hunt, of St Neots Eatons, raised concerns that two parking spaces per home would not be enough and visitors would be forced to park on the road which could lead to a “real highway safety risk”. The Liberal Democrat councillor said: “From our visit to the site there was nowhere on the side of the road that I felt was actually safe for that kind of parking. “It’s a rural road, it’s a 60mph limit and the visibility is not brilliant.” Cllr Jon Neish said that even though cycle parking would be provided at the homes, they’ll still be largely car dependent as they would be “in the middle of nowhere”. The Conservative councillor said: “I wouldn’t want to cycle down there – I was lucky I was on a motorbike at the time, so it was two wheels, but it had an engine. “I just think it’s a little bit awkward myself and I’ve not been convinced that it actually is the right use for this.” Cllr Tom Sanderson said that, since the highway authority didn’t object to the plans, it would be “very difficult” for them to refuse based on parking or road safety concerns. The Liberal Democrat councillor said: “If this went to appeal, the fact is we are in tilted balance – that dreaded phrase. “I think if this were to be rejected, it would be very difficult to justify doing so at appeal.” The application was passed by a single vote with five voting in favour, four against and four abstaining.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: WATCH: Holme Fen wildfire 'unprecedented' says Chief Fire Officer
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: The Chief Fire Officer says that the wildfire at Holme Fen nature reserve in Cambridgeshire is "unprecedented". Matthew Warren, Chief Fire Officer at Cambridgeshire Fire and Rescue, speaking from Holme Fen today (August 20), said that crews could remain at the scene for a number of weeks. Matthew Warren, Chief Fire Officer (Image: Emily Stevens) A blaze broke out at Holme Fen on August 8 and continues to smoulder away, burning up to six metres below the surface deep in the peat. Fire crews from across the country have been on site assisting Cambridgeshire Fire and Rescue Service. Officer Warren said: "I've been with the service 23 years and this is unprecedented, in terms of the resources we have had to deploy, but also the longevity of the incident, because it is going to be ongoing for a few weeks yet. "Clearly we are going to need to have a presence here for a number of weeks to ensure that any hotspots that do materialise we can deal with at that moment in time. "I wouldn't want to put a time limit on it at this time." He added that Natural England will face quite a task to recover from the incident. Officer Warren said: "The nature of our summers now, they are obviously very dry and very hot, which exacerbate the chances of us actually having this type of incident. The blaze broke out at Holme Fen on August 8 (Image: Emily Stevens) "Clearly, I can't say we are going to safeguard against every incident in the future. "But it looks like we are going to get busier, the last three or four years have been extremely busy. "My focus is on ensuring we have the appropriate crews, skills and equipment to deal with these incidents when they do happen."

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: EasyJet has shared a range of European breaks that holidaymakers can take over the August Bank Holiday without taking any annual leave. The airline has unveiled a list of short-haul destinations perfect for a 48-hour getaway, with one-way flights starting at less than £40. Dubbed the “Bank Holiday Loophole,” the idea involves flying out on Friday evening or Saturday morning, returning before Bank Holiday Monday, and still having the day to rest before work resumes. A post shared by easyJet (@easyjet) Tony Hopkins, trading and development director at easyJet holidays, said: "More people are looking to make the most of Bank Holiday weekends, and it’s easy to see why. "A short break offers the chance to switch off, explore somewhere new and enjoy great value, all without using a single day’s annual leave." The concept is designed for those who work a traditional Monday-to-Friday schedule and want to maximise their time off. Destinations on easyJet’s list include Mallorca, Malaga, and Alicante. The airline said it will operate more than 800,000 seats from the UK during the Bank Holiday weekend, a 6% increase compared to last year. Included in this expanded offering are 56 more destinations, including new routes to Preveza in Greece, Reus in Spain, and Ljubljana in Slovenia. Amsterdam and Paris are said to be among the most popular choices for shorter weekend trips. One-way fares begin at £31.99, with a flight from Liverpool to Mallorca. Other options include Manchester to Malaga from £39.99, Birmingham to Gran Canaria from £44.99, and London Luton to Faro from £47.99. Travelers are reminded that these prices are for outbound flights only. They will need to book and pay for a suitable return flight, along with arranging accommodation, transfers, and spending money. St Neots residents have called plans to develop a large car park "disgusting" at a public consultation. The St Neots plan involves turning the Tebbutts Road car park into a neighbourhood with up to 83 homes. A public consultation drop-in session was held in the St Neots Market Square on August 18, where residents could share their views. However, at the event, it was revealed that due to opposition to the plans, it is "unlikely" that the development in St Neots will be going ahead. Residents shared their views on the Tebbutts Road proposals yesterday (August 18) (Image: Emily Stevens) Kimberley, a long-time resident of St Neots, said she felt passionately about the project not going ahead. summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: We tried the lunch menu at newly refurbished Prezzo Italian in Peterborough
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: I was very excited to be invited to Prezzo in Peterborough to try out their lunch menu after their recent refurbishment - and it did not disappoint. Firstly, the restaurant's decor is gorgeous. A member of staff told me they had undergone a complete revamp around six weeks ago to give the space a fresh feel, as before it was apparently a little dark. That certainly isn't a problem anymore; the space feels bright, airy and colourful with modern wood finishes and bold prints on the walls. Prezzo's interior (Image: Emily Stevens) Prezzo's bar (Image: Emily Stevens) My sister and I were seated near the front of the restaurant by the window, but the space is deceivingly large and extends back a long way. There is even a garden space at the back for outdoor dining. Prezzo's outdoor dining space (Image: Emily Stevens) We started off with drinks and both went for one of their homemade coolers. I tried the Wild Strawberry Lemonade, which was delicious, very refreshing and perfect for the unrelenting hot weather we have had this summer. My sister had a Citrus Cooler, which she loved as well and said it was very well presented. Wild Strawberry Lemonade and Citrus Cooler (Image: Emily Stevens) Next we shared the Tomato Bruschetta and some olives to start. We both agreed that the bruschetta was the highlight of the meal; the bread was perfectly crisp but still soft inside and the tomatoes on top were elevated so well by the fresh pesto and balsamic glaze. My sister remarked that the pesto was especially flavourful and we both enjoyed the olives too which came dressed with olive oil and garlic. Olives and Tomato Bruschetta (Image: Emily Stevens) For the main course, I tried one of the specials: the Cheesy Nduja Meatballs and Spaghetti. The pork meatballs were delicious; they were very well seasoned and had a melting cheese centre which I really enjoyed. The pasta tasted freshly made as well, and everything was brought together with a rich tomato sauce that had a bit of a kick from the nduja. Cheesy Nduja Meatballs and Spaghetti (Image: Emily Stevens) My sister was slightly overwhelmed by the size of her vegetable calzone - you definitely get your money's worth with this dish! She liked the marinara dipping sauce it came with and said the dough was excellent; it was finished with a bit of garlic butter and parmesan. However, she did say the vegetable and cheese filling could have been slightly more flavourful. Vegetable Calzone (Image: Emily Stevens) Despite nearly clearing all our plates so far, we decided we had to make room for dessert. I went for the Sicilian Lemon Meringue Pie which was the ideal way to finish. The meringue was perfectly fluffy and complemented the tart lemon filling and buttery pastry very well. Sicilian Lemon Meringue Pie (Image: Emily Stevens) However, I actually preferred my sister's tiramisu which was deliciously creamy and rich. It was a bit of a sweeter take on a classic tiramisu and wasn't overly alcoholic which we enjoyed. Tiramisu (Image: Emily Stevens) Both of us had a great time at Peterborough's Prezzo and will definitely be back. The menu had a huge variety of dishes, from classic Italian pizzas and pastas to different burgers and salads, so there is definitely something for everyone. Expect large portion sizes for main courses though, so be sure to leave room for dessert.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Huntingdon centenarian celebrates milestone birthday with lively party
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A Huntingdon centenarian celebrated her milestone birthday with a lively party. Joan Smith, who turned 100 on August 9, was surrounded by family, friends, and special guests, including the Mayor and Mayoress of Huntingdon. Cromwell House Care Home organised the celebration, which featured a performance by singer Mr Cash and a birthday cake. Joan celebrates 100th birthday surrounded by family and friends (Image: Supplied) Mrs Smith was born in Little Munden, Hertfordshire, in 1926. Due to her father's army career, the family moved around the UK, living at various locations, including Abbey Farm Sawtry, Werrington Farm in Woodwalton, and Manor Farm Barham. During her youth, she resided on the Ramsey Estate, where her father worked for Lord de Ramsey, before settling in Huntingdon in the 1960s. Centenarian marks milestone birthday with special care home party (Image: Supplied) In her younger years, Mrs Smith's family relied on horse and trap as their primary mode of transport. She would walk miles to school and recalled hearing German bombings during the Second World War. At 14, she left school and went into service at The Talbot Hotel in Oundle. Mayor joins celebrations for Joan’s centenary milestone (Image: Supplied) She also served as a civilian volunteer in the Civil Defence. Mrs Smith was married twice and has five children. Her family has grown significantly, and she now has 12 grandchildren, 18 great-grandchildren, and eight great-great-grandchildren. Throughout her life, Mrs Smith has been known for her hard work and love for activities such as horse riding, dog walking, dancing, dressmaking, gardening, and swimming. Family gathers to celebrate Joan’s remarkable 100th birthday (Image: Supplied) Her family expressed their gratitude to the care home, Mr Cash, and the Mayor and Mayoress for making her birthday special. They shared: "Mum has reached an amazing milestone in her life, and we all love her very much." Mrs Smith's family describes her as a "hard0working" woman who has enjoyed various hobbies throughout her life.

The Comet's airworthy future appeared uncertain, but Shuttleworth has now confirmed it will repair the damage and return it to flight. summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Shocking figures reveal cruelty against wild birds in Cambridgeshire
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Startling new figures have revealed the number of reports of cruelty involving wild birds in Cambridgeshire. Released by the RSPCA, the data shows the charity has received its highest number of cruelty reports across the UK in five years. Lethal weapons such as catapults, slingshots and airguns have been used in the horrific attacks against wild birds. Across the UK, 359 incidents involving wild birds were reported during July and August 2025 - almost double the 179 reports received during the same period in 2024. The data also shows the RSPCA received 40 per cent all reports of cruelty towards wild birds during the summer months last year. Longer days and increased time spent outdoors are all thought to be contributing factors, the charity said. The birds most commonly targeted last year include pigeons, corvids (such as crows, magpies and ravens), gulls, swans and ducks. In Cambridgeshire alone, the charity received eight reports of cruelty involving wild birds. While there is no single explanation for the overall rise, the RSPCA believes a range of factors may contribute to deliberate attacks on wildlife. These can include deliberate misuse of catapults and air weapons, copycat behaviour, greater exposure to harmful online content, and a lack of understanding about animal welfare. Mike Scargill, wildlife partnerships manager for the RSPCA said: "We are deeply concerned by the number of reports involving deliberate cruelty towards wild birds. "Day after day, our frontline officers and animal centres see the sickening consequences of weapons being used on animals - causing awful suffering, severe injuries and often leading to death. "These figures are likely to represent only a fraction of the true scale of the problem because a lot of cruelty goes unseen and unreported. "This is why we need our supporters to back our Cruelty Hurts Love Rescue campaign so we can tackle this horrific trend." He added: "Wild birds feel pain, fear and distress, and deserve our care and respect. "Deliberately harming them causes immense suffering and can have devastating consequences for both individual animals and local wildlife populations." Have you got a story you want to share? It is understood the official "confirmed" asylum seekers will move into the addresses, although this could not be independently verified. Concerns have been raised about the suitability of the properties, which are located in close proximity to vulnerable residents. We've got a lot of elderly people round here and we do not want this," one local claimed. "I know they've got to live somewhere. We're all God's children at the end of the day and I don't wish them any harm. "But what we're concerned about is that myself and my neighbour are vulnerable and the top and middle flats overlook our garden." Councillor Stephen Ferguson said the wider community had not "been given the information they need to plan ahead". He added: "The priority now is for Serco, the council, the police, local services, community groups and residents to work together. "We need to keep everyone safe, make sure the right plans are in place and give people clear facts instead of leaving rumours to spread." "St Neots is a strong and welcoming community. If we share the facts, speak calmly and work together, we can deal with this in a sensible and responsible way." Serco said it does not confirm the addresses of properties it may rent for asylum accommodation. A spokesperson said: "We work under the direction of the Home Office, who decide where people are placed, based on overall national demand." Despite this, Cambridgeshire Constabulary said it had "been notified by partners and are engaging with them". Huntingdonshire District Council said it was aware of "speculation" regarding "potential asylum accommodation in the Eynesbury ward of St Neots." A spokesperson said: "Decisions about asylum accommodation are the responsibility of the Home Office and its accommodation providers. "While the council may be consulted and can raise local concerns where appropriate, it does not make these decisions. "It would not be appropriate for the council to comment on, verify, or speculate about reports relating to specific properties or individuals. They added: "Any confirmation should come from the Home Office or the relevant accommodation provider. "We encourage residents to rely on trusted, official sources and avoid sharing unverified information." The Home Office has been contacted for comment. Have you got a story you want to share? The warning comes just days before GCSE results day on Thursday, August 20, when hundreds of thousands of teenagers will decide what to do next. If a teenager is continuing in qualifying non-advanced education or approved training, parents can extend their Child Benefit claim. But if they fail to respond by the deadline, payments will stop automatically. More than 372,000 parents have already extended their claims digitally. Parents can complete the process in just a few minutes using the HMRC app or GOV.UK. Those who received a letter from HMRC can also scan the QR code to access the service. Child Benefit is currently worth up to £1,406.60 a year for the eldest or only child, or £930.80 for each additional child. Myrtle Lloyd, HMRC's Chief Customer Officer, said: “Exam results season is a big moment for teenagers deciding their next steps, and it's the perfect time for parents to confirm those plans with us. “Child Benefit is a vital source of support for many families and we don't want anyone to miss out. It only takes a few minutes using the HMRC app or GOV.UK, so make sure you’re receiving the payments you're entitled to.” Child Benefit can continue while a young person remains in full-time, non-advanced education, including: Parents only need to act if their teenager is starting a new qualifying course or training in September. Those already partway through a course that HMRC has previously been told about do not need to contact them. Recommended reading: However, Child Benefit does not continue for children doing a university degree, a standard apprenticeship in England, or a course forming part of a job contract. Parents must also tell HMRC if their child's circumstances change, such as leaving education or starting a paid apprenticeship, to avoid being overpaid. summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: E-bikes confiscated by police in Cambs increased by 1,400% in a year
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: The number of e-bikes confiscated by Cambridgeshire Police has increased by more than 1,400% in the last year, data reveals. According to data obtained by the Press Association under freedom-of-information laws, the force seized 126 e-bikes between April 2025 and March 2026. This was up from only eight between April 2024 and March 2025, an increase of 1,475%. The increase is also a pattern across the UK. 7,049 e-bikes were confiscated across the UK in the 12 months to May 19. During the previous year, there were only 3,858 confiscated, an increase of 83%. The sharp increase in confiscations has led to renewed calls for tougher laws, with campaigners warning that illegal e-bikes pose a risk to pedestrians and other road users. Across the UK, police e-bike confiscations have increased by 83% (Image: Ben Whitley/PA Wire) Labour MP for Carlisle Julie Minns, who has proposed a ban on sales of illegal e-bikes and conversion kits, said they should be defined as an “unsafe product” which cannot be sold by online retailers. She said: "I think an illegal e-bike is an unsafe product and I think the Government should designate illegal e-bikes so that the ones that don’t meet the definition and the kits that create them that don’t meet the definition of a legal e-bike, designate those an unsafe product and say to retailers you can no longer sell them." Earlier this year the Department for Business and Trade sought views on product safety reforms, including considering tougher rules on e-bike batteries and conversion kits, to crack down on illegal modifications. The department is expected to publish its response to the consultation next month. It comes after the All-Party Parliamentary Group for Cycling and Walking (APPGCW) last year warned of a “crisis hiding in plain sight” as it published a report which found the rise of illegal and unsafe e-bikes was putting lives at risk. Richard Dilks, chief executive of shared transport charity CoMoUK, said there is “a growing enforcement challenge” in relation to illegal e-bikes. He went on: “This challenge would be easier to meet if we had up-to-date laws across low-powered, small zero emission vehicles, which could then be enforced from the point of retail onwards. “It is time to end the delays and take action now.” The Government said it has changed the law to strengthen police powers for e-bike seizures.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: New chair appointed to lead board of Cambs charity
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Share A new chair has been appointed to lead the board of a Cambridgeshire charity. Andrew Glover now heads Caring Together Charity, taking over from Stuart Evans following his retirement at the end of a nine-year term. Mr Evans played a key role in shaping the charity’s development and growth and stepped down during a board meeting held today. He said: "I shall miss it, but it’s amazing to realise it's been nine years. "It doesn't feel as if it's been that long, but it’s nice to reflect on how the charity has changed in that time. "I think Andrew is going to be terrific as chair. "I’m confident the charity is well positioned for the future under new leadership with a refreshed strategy, strong governance and a continued commitment to support carers." During his time as chair, Mr Evans oversaw major milestones including appointing chief executive Miriam Martin, a rebrand, office relocations, and the charity’s response to the Covid-19 pandemic. Caring Together Charity supports unpaid carers across Cambridgeshire, Peterborough and Norfolk. Mr Glover, who joined the board of trustees in March 2026, is a business leader with experience in the IT and telecommunications sectors. He said: "Caring Together is a meaningful charity with a very valid purpose, which is why I wanted to get involved. "The charity is in really good shape and that’s largely because of Stuart and Miriam’s leadership. "I’m looking forward to helping Caring Together build on these strong foundations as it strives to reach and support even more unpaid carers." Mr Glover also brings personal experience of caring, having helped look after his mother-in-law, who had Alzheimer’s. Ms Martin welcomed the new appointment. She said: "We are delighted to welcome Andrew Glover as Stuart’s successor. "We look forward to working with him over the coming years." Share

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Residents lead effort to tackle speeding and make roads safer
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Share Residents are taking the lead in making their roads safer by tackling speeding head-on. In Cambridgeshire, more than 1,000 volunteers are involved in the Community Speedwatch scheme, which aims to reduce speeding and promote safer driving through community action and support from the police. Central to the scheme’s success is Julie Clark, the force-wide Watch Coordination Officer, who has dedicated nearly two years to supporting volunteers, coordinating schemes, and addressing community concerns. Ms Clark said: "Being part of the Vision Zero initiative means so much. "To be given joint responsibility with my team to help reduce the number of people killed or seriously injured on Cambridgeshire's roads is a privilege. "I am so grateful to members of the community who volunteer their free time to help keep Cambridgeshire's roads safe." Community Speedwatch now operates in 113 groups across the county, with four additional HGV Watch schemes. Trained volunteers monitor vehicle speeds and gather data in areas where speeding is a concern. Their work contributes to educating drivers and providing valuable information to police and road safety partners. Police and Crime Commissioner Darryl Preston, who chairs the Cambridgeshire and Peterborough Vision Zero Partnership, said: "Every death or serious injury on our roads is one too many. "Community Speedwatch demonstrates what can be achieved when local people, volunteers, and partner organisations work together towards a common goal. "Julie’s passion and commitment, alongside the incredible dedication shown by our volunteers, is helping create safer roads across Cambridgeshire. "As chair of the Vision Zero board, I remain committed to investing in practical initiatives that educate drivers, reduce speeding, and ultimately save lives." The initiative is supported by the commissioner’s Vision Zero safety vans, which serve as a visible deterrent and reinforce the importance of driving safely. Parish councils, community groups, or residents interested in starting a scheme can contact Julie Clark at speedwatch@cambs.police.uk. Share

Work has begun on a major new sport and health hub in Huntingdonshire, supported by a £30 million investment. The refurbishment of Huntingdon Leisure Centre was granted planning permission by the district council's development management committee in February. The new Huntingdon Sport and Health Hub will be developed at the site, with construction now underway as of July 2026. A new 3G Football pitch is expected to be completed by autumn 2026 and forms part of a £30 million investment in the wider hub. The new hub promises to deliver expanded swimming facilities, improved health and fitness centres, and new outdoor sports areas. Councillor Debbie Mickelburgh, executive member for communities, health and leisure at Huntingdonshire District Council, said: "After years of planning and collaboration with our partners, it is fantastic to see work now underway on site. "This development will create modern, accessible facilities that support healthier lifestyles, improve wellbeing and provide opportunities for people of all ages to be active." Work has officially begun at the new hub as of July 2026 (Image: HDC) The plans for the hub are part of Huntingdonshire District Council's wider aim to help tackle the shortage of swimming and fitness provision across the district. The council wants to make it easier for people of all ages to stay active locally. The councillors for Huntingdon North ward, Cllr David Henly, Cllr Steve Lancaster and Cllr Michael Simpson, said: “This is an important moment for Huntingdon. "For many years residents have known that the existing swimming facilities were reaching the end of their useful life, and this week we are finally seeing diggers on the ground and the new wider facility beginning to become a reality. "This is not simply about replacing an old swimming pool. "It is about giving Huntingdon a leisure centre capable of serving families, swimmers, sports clubs and residents for decades to come.” The overall programme will continue through to autumn 2028 and includes a new main hub building, padel and pickleball courts, as well as upgrades to existing facilities. summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Holme Fen fire continues to burn as fire service issues update
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Share Share Firefighters are continuing to tackle a blaze at a Cambridgeshire nature reserve that has now been burning for more than a week. Crews were first called to the blaze at Holme Fen Nature Reserve, in Holme, at 10.24am on August 8. Crews from Dogsthorpe, Stanground, the north roaming fire engine, Whittlesey, Huntingdon, Thorney, St Neots, Ramsey and Sawston attended. The fire has now been burning for more than a week, but Cambridgeshire Fire and Rescue said that crews are expected to remain at the scene "for the foreseeable future". In a statement from today (August 17), the fire service said crews are still working to extinguish the fire. Wayne Swales, area commander at Cambridgeshire Fire and Rescue Service, said: "Although temperatures have reduced from during the week, it has still been hot on the fireground, but crews have stood up to the challenge exceptionally. The fire service said crews are still working to extinguish the fire (Image: Cambridgeshire Fire and Rescue) "Thanks to the fantastic teamwork from all crews across the county and the incredible support from our National Resilience colleagues from all over the country, we look to be a better position. "Steady progress has been made and we are discussing our tactics regularly to try and hopefully start to scale back our firefighting. "We will know more over the next day or so." Mr Swales said the service has been "overwhelmed" by support from the public and thanked everyone who has donated. He also praised partner agencies for their assistance, particularly Natural England.  The fire follows a recent Government emergency alert warning of increased wildfire risk on Friday (August 14). Residents are being urged to stay vigilant and help reduce the risk of further fires. The fire service has advised the public to dispose of cigarettes safely, take litter home, avoid barbecues and bonfires, and not use fireworks. Emergency lines should be kept clear for real emergencies. People are advised to call 999 only if they see a fire that is spreading, out of control, or poses an immediate risk to life or property. summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: St Neots traders praise council takeover but call for advertisement of market days
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Share Share Traders have urged Huntingdonshire District Council to better advertise market days as they fight to adapt to changing shopping trends. St Neots Market, held every Thursday in the Market Square, was taken over by Huntingdonshire District Council in November. It followed a multi-million-pound refurbishment of the square which was closed for over a year while works were carried out. Phil Anderson has been trading at St Neots for around 20 years, and said the market has improved since the council took it over. The 70-year-old said: “The improvements have been very good, footfall has increased dramatically which is surprising considering the town is losing its shops rapidly. It normally drops when the kids go on holiday but it hasn’t been too bad.” Richard McCann first set up on the market square about five months ago but before that was trading in other markets across the country. The 62-year-old said the market could be advertised better on social media. He said: “I think it does help – I do a pub car park in Bournemouth and I’m mobbed, they’re quite good on social media.” One trader, who did not want to be named, said that trade is tough but it’s “nothing to do with the council”. He said: “Shops and banks are closing – we bounce off the shops and they bounce off us. All the rates, national insurance, it’s ridiculous.” Emma, who did not give her surname, said that free parking could help to attract customers to the market square. She said: “There’s no free parking here at all – if they made the first hour free I think that would help.” Mathew Thornton was a trader at Huntingdon market when he was told a spot was available at St Neots and decided to give it a go. The 46-year-old said: “The weather is unbearable but the footfall is just the same for me.” Jimmy Singh has been trading at the market for 38 years and said he’s seen a “hell of a lot of change” with “not even a quarter” of traders left. The 72-year-old said: “We need more traders in the market – we have seven stalls and it’s not enough. It used to be in a big square like this, you would have more than 60 traders.” Read more Work begins on new £30 million Hunts sport and health hub New chair appointed to lead board of Cambs charity 10 road closures in Cambridgeshire you should be aware of this week Paul Firman, the market’s “longest serving green grocer”, said the council does what they can to help but markets everywhere are struggling. The 66-year-old said: “They don’t do a bad job but the market has changed since Covid – people’s shopping habits have changed. “What can be done – what can be done about the high street? They aren’t doing a bad job – the rent is reasonable and they look after you. It’s a shame the way things are going but it’s the same with pubs – this country is built on small businesses. When I first came here 38 years ago there were five green grocers and the market was absolutely buzzing, but so was every market.” He also said the council could advertise Thursday’s market better – like they do for the farmer’s market, held twice a month. Huntingdonshire District Council have been approached for comment. Share

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Share The family of a teen biker who died in a crash outside a pub in Cambridgeshire have paid tribute to their "darling boy". Holton Knott, 19, tragically died when his black Honda 599cc motorbike was involved in a collision with a silver Jaguar XF. It happened at around 8.50pm on Tuesday (August 11) outside the Green Man pub on the A1309, High Street, Trumpington. Knott, of Doddington Road, Chatteris, was taken to Addenbrooke’s Hospital but died there the following day. The Jaguar driver, a 69-year-old man from Cambridge, was arrested on suspicion of causing death by careless/inconsiderate driving. He has been bailed until November 11. Holton’s parents said in a statement: "On the evening of 11 August, we received the unimaginable news that our darling boy was involved in a horrific accident. "After a great effort from all the team at Addenbrooke’s Hospital, it was clear Holton wasn't going to survive. "We appreciate the kind-hearted messages and offers of support by many a friend and family member. Thanks again for your support in these tough times. "Unfortunately Holton gained his wings at 11am on Wednesday. Forever 19 and forever loved." Officers are still appealing for information and dashcam footage from anyone who may have witnessed the collision or the vehicles in the time leading up to it. Have you got a story you want to share?
