summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: 88-year-old care home resident’s dream comes true seeing favourite singer live
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Share Share An 88-year-old who lives in Huntingdon has had her dream come true after seeing her favourite singer perform live on stage. Doreen Cousins, a resident at The Chase care home, was surprised with tickets to see Alfie Boe in concert at the Cambridge Corn Exchange, just 30 minutes from her home. Ms Cousins has long expressed her love for Mr Boe’s music and often talked about how much she would love to see him perform in person. Natalie doing her magic (Image: Supplied) Karina, a senior carer at The Chase who accompanied Ms Cousins to the concert, said: "I just loved being part of such a special evening. "Doreen has talked often about how much she adores Alfie Boe, and seeing the excitement on her face when she realised she was finally going was wonderful to see. "For me, that’s one of the most rewarding parts of working in care: helping people do things they have always wanted to but may have thought were no longer possible." Doreen and her daughter (Image: Supplied) The team at The Chase arranged an accessible ticket and transport for Ms Cousins and her daughter, who initially worried that the journey might be too much. The outing was kept a complete surprise until the last moment. Ms Cousins said: "I had the best time, so much fun." Her daughter added: "Wow, oh my goodness, I can’t believe it. Alfie Boe performing (Image: Supplied) "It was great – she loved it." Lauren Mair, general manager at The Chase, said: "Music can play a hugely important role in later life, helping people reconnect with memories, emotions and the things they love most. "When we saw how much Alfie Boe’s music meant to Doreen, the team was determined to do everything we could to help her see him perform live. "I’m incredibly proud of the staff for going the extra mile to make such a special memory possible." Share

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Man strangled and grabbed ex-partner by hair in 'violent' attack
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Share A man who followed and strangled his ex-partner in a violent attack has been jailed. Fred Lamb, 43, targeted the woman as she cycled past the Grafton Centre car park in Cambridge at around 6pm on February 23. He called out to her, but she ignored him and continued cycling. Lamb then followed her on his own bike, repeatedly shouting her name. He followed her into Discovery Way, where he deliberately crashed the front wheel of his bike into hers, causing her to fall. He then got on top of her and shouted: "Give me your money". The victim tried to escape, but Lamb grabbed her by the hair and searched her pockets. When she pushed him away, he bit her fingers. CCTV audio captured the victim telling him: "I'm not coming with you, let go of me. "Just go, just go." She was later heard saying: "Please, you're being nasty," before screaming: "He's biting me, help, help." The woman managed to break free and ran towards a nearby address. As she reached the front door, Lamb placed his hands around her neck and squeezed. Two members of the public intervened, shouting that they were calling the police. They told Lamb to leave the victim alone and he walked away from the scene. Officers arrived and found Lamb hiding in a bush on a nearby street, where he was arrested. At Peterborough Crown Court on Thursday, August 13, Lamb, of no fixed abode in the Cambridge area, was sentenced to one year and four months in prison. He after pleaded guilty to intentional strangulation. A charge of assault with intent to commit robbery was ordered to lie on file. Detective Constable Edward McAuley said: "This was a terrifying attack on a woman who was simply trying to go about her day. "Lamb repeatedly targeted the victim, assaulted her and then strangled her as she desperately tried to get away from him. "Strangulation is an extremely serious offence which can have devastating and long-lasting physical and psychological effects. "I would like to commend the victim for her bravery throughout the investigation and thank the members of the public who stepped in to help and contacted police. "I hope this sentence demonstrates that we will pursue offenders and do everything we can to protect victims from violence and abuse." Have you got a story you want to share? summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Share An amber weather warning for extreme heat has been issued across Cambridgeshire tomorrow (August 13), with temperatures expected to sore to 35°. The Met Office is telling people to "keep yourself safe", warning that "health effects are likely to be experienced by those vulnerable to extreme heat". The amber warning is in place from 9am until 11.59pm tomorrow, with the warning having a medium likelihood and a medium impact. "Keep yourself safe by following these simple steps to reduce the likelihood of the heat making you feel unwell," the Met Office said. "Drink plenty of fluids, keep out of the sun and avoid any exercise between 11am and 3pm when the sun is strongest and close curtains in rooms that face the sun. "If you are going out take water with you, stay in the shade, wear sunscreen and a wide brimmed hat. "Give yourself the best chance of avoiding delays by checking road conditions if driving, or bus and train timetables, amending your travel plans if necessary. "If using public transport, there are many simple things you can do to keep yourself safe. Carry water with you, take a small hand-held battery powered fan. "If you feel unwell get off at next stop for some fresh air, dress in light fabrics in light colours to help stay cooler, keep an eye on fellow passengers for signs they may be struggling." Share

Run-down barns on the farm where Tony Martin shot and killed a teenage burglar in the Fens can be turned into homes. West Norfolk Council has agreed plans to convert two of the buildings close to Bleak House, where Mr Martin turned his unlicensed shotgun on 16-year-old Fred Barras in August, 1999. His death sparking a national debate over how much force householders could use to defend their homes. The proposals were submitted by Jacqui and David Wadsley, to whom Mr Martin left his £2.5m estate including the farm at Emneth Hungate, near Wisbech, after he passed away at the age of 80 in February, 2025. They include turning two buildings into four homes, comprising two four-bedroom houses, one three-bedroom home and one five-bedroom property. Barns at Cow Croft Field Farm can be converted into homes (Image: Chris Bishop) An architect's drawing showing how one of the barns would look after being converted (Image: Swann Edwards) Police outside one of the barns which can now be converted into homes (Image: Newsquest) Earlier plans for 10 new houses were withdrawn after officials raised concerns over their impact on wildlife. But the smaller scheme qualified for so-called permitted development rights, which allow farm buildings to be converted into housing without going through the full planning process. An ecological survey concluded it would have a "negligible" impact on protected species such as bats and badgers. The application stated that converting the barns would not increase traffic compared to their previous agricultural use. Fred Barras, 16, who died in the shootings at Bleak House (Image: PA) Jacqui and David Wadsley, who have inherited Tony Martin's farm at Emneth Hungate in west Norfolk (Image: Facebook) A drawing showing the layout of the site (Image: Swann Edwards) Bleak House itself, which no stands derelict is not part of the development. The farm was owned by Mr Martin, who made headlines in 1999 for fatally shooting Mr Barras and wounding his accomplice Brendan Fearon. He was found guilty of murder the following year but the conviction was reduced to manslaughter on appeal in October 2001. In February, it was revealed that Mr Martin had left his £2.5 million estate to Mrs Wadsley, who ran the Hare and Hounds pub in Wisbech where he drank, after he was released from prison in 2003. Tony Martin's Bleak House property was boarded up after the shootings (Image: Matthew Usher) The 164-acre Cow Croft Field Farm at Emneth Hungate, formerly owned by Tony Martin, is being sold via Cruso & Wilkin with a guide price totalling £1.378m (Image: Cruso & Wilkin) Some 164 acres of land around the farm, originally named Cow Croft Field Farm, has now been put up for sale in two lots for £1.37m. Mrs Wadsley said it was an opportunity for someone to do the farm justice. Share

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: MP pushes for energy-saving homes scheme after bill-free house visit
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Share Share A Huntingdonshire MP is calling for urgent action to help residents improve the energy efficiency of their homes. Ian Sollom, Liberal Democrat MP for St Neots and Mid Cambridgeshire, is urging the government to introduce an energy-saving homes scheme. The call comes following a visit to the Oakington home of Paul Kershaw, which has operated without energy bills for seven years thanks to extensive retrofitting and renewable technology. Mr Sollom said: "I was really impressed with Paul’s house and the retrofit and sustainability measures he has put in place. "His commitment to sharing his knowledge and helping others make their homes more sustainable is truly inspiring. "His experience has made him a strong advocate for higher standards, better training and stronger consumer protection within the retrofit and heat pump sectors." Mr Kershaw’s home features solar panels, a 60kWh battery, and vehicle-to-grid technology that allows his electric car to power the house. He now volunteers with the Cambridge Retrofit Hub and gives talks to residents and contractors on energy efficiency. Mr Sollom and the Liberal Democrats are calling for an energy-saving homes scheme to identify the most effective combination of tax incentives, loans and grants, together with advice and support. Ian with constituent Paul Kershaw at his home in Oakington (Image: Supplied) They are also advocating for a 10-year emergency upgrade programme, prioritising free insulation and heat pumps for low-income households, and ensuring all new homes meet zero-carbon standards. Mr Sollom said: "The Government needs to do much more to help people make their homes energy efficient by introducing the energy-saving homes scheme. "It is also vital that if the UK is to meet the 2050 energy targets, we must ensure more people have the skills that the construction industry needs and that these are of a good standard." Mr Kershaw said the benefits of a healthier, zero-bill home were immediate, though not without challenges. Share

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Share Find, save and share Public Notices that affect you in the  area. The Public Notice Portal carries statutory public notices published in local newspapers and is the fastest and most effective way of finding out what is happening in YOUR neighbourhood. A temporary solar farm has been approved in the Cambridgeshire countryside despite fears it will harm the green belt. The development would also include a battery energy storage facility and developers Innova Renewables said it could power around 13,422 homes annually. They said the panels would deliver up to 49.99MW of renewable energy and 10MW could be stored. South Cambridgeshire District Council’s planning committee considered the application for a 40-year operational period, after which the site would be restored to agricultural use. Concerns had been raised about the 74 hectare site off Low Fen Drove Way in Horningsea’s impact on nearby Grade-II listed Biggin Abbey. The proposal is also next to a site where the sewage treatment works in Cambridge was set to be relocated – but the future of this is unclear after the government withdrew funding. The application was recommended for approval by council officers who said it would be “temporary and low scale” and considered the land to be grey belt – a site considered to make only a limited contribution to the green belt. John Hughes, from the National Trust, said that “significant opportunities” were missed in the application to improve biodiversity and nature recovery. He said: “With a close proximity to Cambridge and other local populations, an opportunity to better connect with people and nature has been missed along with the varied social benefits it would provide.” Although the scheme “substantially exceeds” the requirement for biodiversity net gain, Mr Hughes said this was largely through “passive measures” like the conversion of arable land to grassland. He said: “For a development of this scale on green belt land we would have expected a more ambitious and integrated approach to nature recovery.” An agent for the developer said the scheme had “significant benefits” and would support “both local and national renewable energy and decarbonisation targets”. She said: “South Cambridgeshire Council declared a climate emergency in 2019 and this year’s climate and nature strategy committed to a 50 per cent reduction by 2030 and net zero by 2050 for area wide emissions. “This is well evident in the climate conditions we’re seeing across the UK and Europe this week.” Councillor Anna Bradnam, speaking as ward councillor for Milton and Waterbeach, said that although the scheme is described as temporary, “40 years is half a lifetime”. The Liberal Democrat councillor said: “I respect the officer’s view but regret that the green belt protections which used to be so strong have been eroded by this concept of grey belt. “I believe this development would have a degrading and industrialising impact on the countryside in this area – how can 74 hectares of glass and metal for 40 years be considered a minor adverse impact?” Cllr Vivien Biggs, of Swavesey, said that the development couldn’t be argued to enhance the area, but they had to consider balance. The Liberal Democrat councillor said: “I think we have to be pragmatic, and obviously anybody having something like this in their back yard is not going to be particularly happy. “It’s not beautiful, but we also know we don’t own the view unless we own the land.” Cllr Heather Williams, of The Mordens, also said that planning was about “trade-offs” and there will never be a “perfect solution”. The Conservative councillor said: “There’s merit for it in its objectives but, in my view, there’s a lot of policies it comes into conflict with. “I think we need more renewable energy and I 100 per cent understand why farming communities are looking to things like solar in the current situation – but there are alternative places.” The solar farm was approved with four voting in favour and one against. Share

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Share Share A Cambridgeshire man has been jailed for more than two years after a"prolonged and violent attack" on his partner. Callum Liddle, 38, of no fixed abode but from the Peterborough area, flew into a rage after his partner received a text message from another man on July 19 last year. As she stood up from a chair, he blocked her exit, pushed her, and physically assaulted her. He grabbed her by the hair, pushed her into bookshelves, threw her to the floor, and kicked her in the back three times. Liddle then pinned her down with his knees on her chest, covered her nose and mouth, and poured cider over her face while she struggled to breathe. The victim managed to hit him with an object and escape the attack. Callum Liddle flew into a rage after his partner received a message from another man (Image: Cambridgeshire Police) Detective Constable Kate Jacklin said: "This was a prolonged and violent attack during which Liddle repeatedly assaulted the victim and deliberately restricted her breathing. "His actions demonstrated a complete disregard for her safety and left her fearing for her life. "Domestic abuse can have a devastating and long-lasting impact on victims, but we are committed to supporting those affected and bringing offenders before the courts." Liddle pleaded guilty to intentional suffocation and assault occasioning actual bodily harm (ABH), as well as assault by beating relating to a separate incident involving another victim in May last year. He was sentenced to two years and seven months in prison at Peterborough Crown Court on August 7 and was given a ten-year restraining order. Charges of threats to damage property, threats to kill, and intentional strangulation were ordered to lie on file. Anyone experiencing domestic abuse can report it to police via 101 or online. Always call 999 in an emergency. Share

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Meet owner of award-nominated Hunts photography business
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Share Share A decade of capturing precious moments has turned a passion for photography into a thriving business. St Ives-based Dinky Little Dot Photography is celebrating 10 years of specialising in newborn and baby photography, offering families timeless portraits and lasting memories. Founded and run by Laura, the studio creates a calm, welcoming space for newborn, maternity, baby milestone, cake smash and family photography sessions in St Ives, Cambridgeshire. Laura said: "Photography has always been something I’ve loved, but after seeing just how quickly babies change during those first few weeks of life, I realised how important it is to preserve those memories. "I wanted to build a business that gives families beautiful, lasting reminders of moments that pass by so quickly." Since launching under different branding in 2012 and transitioning to specialist newborn photography in 2016, Laura has photographed hundreds of babies and families from Huntingdonshire, Cambridgeshire, Suffolk, and beyond. The business stands out for its exclusive focus on newborn and baby photography, alongside a commitment to safety, experience and comfort. Laura said: "I’ve invested heavily in specialist training, professional equipment and creating a luxury studio experience where parents can simply relax while I take care of everything. "My aim isn’t just to provide digital photographs – it’s to create artwork that becomes part of a family’s home and tells their story for years to come." Dinky Little Dot Photography is independently owned and operated, with Laura handling every client interaction from initial enquiry to final artwork delivery. She is occasionally supported by a contracted colleague during peak times for viewing appointments. The business is the focus of this week’s Think Local / Buy Local campaign. Laura said: "Supporting local businesses has such a positive impact on our community. "When people choose independent businesses, they’re supporting local families, helping create local jobs and keeping money within the local economy. "As a small business owner, I’m incredibly grateful every time a family chooses me to capture such an important chapter in their lives. "Those decisions allow independent businesses like mine to continue growing, investing back into the local community and providing a personal service that larger companies simply can’t replicate." This milestone year has been especially rewarding for Laura, who has also been named a finalist in two categories at the Huntingdonshire Business Awards: Small Business of the Year and St Ives Business of the Year. She was also a finalist in the Small Business of the Year category last year. Laura said: "It’s a real honour to receive that recognition and a reflection of the wonderful support I’ve received from local families over the last decade. "I’m incredibly proud to be part of the Huntingdonshire business community and look forward to welcoming many more families into the studio in the years ahead." Dinky Little Dot Photography is based at 1st Floor, 8 Harding Way, St Ives, Cambridgeshire, PE27 3WR. To find out more or to book a session, visit www.dinkylittledot.co.uk or email laura@dinkylittledot.co.uk. Share

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Hunts cancer charity receives 'generous' donation
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Share A charity helping cancer survivors has been given a "generous" donation. Hunts Community Cancer Network (HCCN), which supports adults living with or beyond cancer in Huntingdonshire, was awarded £7,899 from NFU Mutual's Huntingdon Agency. Representatives from the agency visited one of the charity's weekly Get Active sessions in St Neots to see how the money will help improve the wellbeing of cancer survivors. HCCN’s Get Active programme offers free physical activity opportunities across Huntingdonshire to help adults prepare for treatment, recover afterwards, or adjust to life beyond cancer. The sessions take place across Huntingdonshire in various community spaces, including HCCN’s weekly drop-in groups in Sawtry, St Neots, and the Lady Olivia Centre in Brampton. Specialist exercise classes are also held in partnership with One Leisure, as well as other movement-based activities throughout the week. The One Leisure classes are free to attend, with no membership required. HCCN's Get Active sessions form part of its Move, Mood, Food approach to wellbeing, recognising the importance of physical activity, emotional wellbeing, and healthy lifestyle choices before, during, and after cancer treatment. As more people are living with and beyond cancer, demand for community-based wellbeing services continues to grow. HCCN now supports nearly 800 adults across Huntingdonshire through Get Active classes, support groups, counselling, complementary therapies, and practical information. The donation was given to HCCN through the NFU Mutual Agency Giving Fund, a national initiative that distributed £2.33 million to frontline charities across the UK during 2026. By inviting local agencies to nominate charities making a positive difference within their communities, the fund helps ensure support reaches organisations where it can have the greatest impact. To explore HCCN’s full Get Active programme, view the latest activities timetable or register your interest, visit: hccnthecharity.org/ouroffer. Share

Plans for a retirement home on land allocated for a pub in a town residents said “desperately” needs more places to meet have been refused. Central Cambourne had few pieces of land left undeveloped when the application was decided, with the area next to the Holiday Inn Express off Back Lane one of them. Permission for a restaurant and pub had been granted for the site, but it was still empty when the 58 retired living apartments were proposed. McCarthy Stone Retirement Lifestyles Limited claimed the scheme would provide “much needed” retirement accommodation in the area. But one resident, in a written objection submitted to South Cambridgeshire District Council, said there were “still many unsold McCarthy Stone retirement flats in their other Cambourne developments”. They said that since the site was the “last available space” in the town centre it could have a “big impact on the community” which is “already lacking amenities”. Another written objection said: “The last thing Cambourne needs is another retirement development. “There are thousands of people now living in the various Cambourne sections with more development being carried out. There is nowhere for people to go, nothing to do, and the one GP surgery is struggling; one pub, one coffee shop. “My view is that another retirement block will do nothing to enhance the town.” The council’s planning committee were asked to decide on the application, which they were recommended to refuse, on Wednesday (August 12). Julie Ayer, speaking on behalf of Cambourne Town Council, said the design of the development “simply doesn’t fit”. She said: “Cambourne is a vibrant, active community which embraces development and accepts and encourages change – but not at any cost. “Unfortunately, the application before you today is not one of a quality that Cambourne Town Council feel they can support for several reasons. “The design and form of this proposed development is poor and doesn’t enhance the character or have any social inclusion benefits within it.” Cllr Helene Leeming, speaking as a ward councillor for Cambourne, said the site was “one of the last unallocated parcels of land” in the town centre. The Liberal Democrat councillor said: “A town that desperately wants more places where people can meet and spend leisure time. “Earlier plans to build a pub there were supported, but a residential block like this removes the opportunity for this piece of land to be available to the community. “Cambourne needs more than just housing to thrive.” She said that 61 residents had written to object to the scheme, and said the design was “overcrowded, uninteresting and blocky”. Cllr Michael Booth, also of Cambourne, added that the development would be “fundamentally unsafe”. The Liberal Democrat councillor said: “The lack of provision of adequate crossings for elderly residents would inhibit their access to daily services without asking them to take risks on their own safety on a regular basis.” The application was unanimously rejected by the planning committee. Share People in Cambridgeshire and Peterborough spend the most on prescriptions, nearly £380 per person each year, new data reveals. A new study by Cured Pharmacy has revealed that the Cambridgeshire and Peterborough Integrated Care Board (ICB) tops the national ranking for prescription spending, totalling £401,425,034 for a population of 1,056,872. This works out to £379.82 per person—the highest in the country. Despite not having the highest prescription volume, the cost per item is the most expensive in England at £17.12. Tarun Kumar, co-founder and superintendent pharmacist of Cured Pharmacy, said: "What stands out is the enormous variation across England. "Cambridgeshire and Peterborough spends more than three times per person what North West London does, and that gap is largely driven by the cost of individual prescriptions rather than the volume. "This could reflect differences in the types of medications being prescribed, such as higher proportions of specialist or newer treatments in certain areas." summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Cambridge South has halved journey times say NHS staff
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Share Share NHS staff said Cambridge’s newest station has already halved commutes while debate remains around its lack of parking. Cambridge South station is connected to the city’s cycle network and next to the guided busway system, with Trumpington Park and Ride (P&R) less than 20 minutes away. Though there isn’t any general parking for commuters – unlike the main station which has hundreds of spaces – there are five blue-badge bays for those with disabilities and space for pick-up and drop-offs. The station first opened its doors to passengers on June 28 with trains to London, Birmingham, and Stansted Airport. Kinga Bozek, who lives in Trumpington, said she likes the new station but there could be more regular bus connections to the park and ride. The 47-year-old said: “I would like more connections and buses later on because when you come back later there’s a bus every 30 minutes, and it’s a 30 minute walk. “There should be parking to be honest – or more buses to Trumpington Park and Ride if they want to go for that. “But it’s better to come here even if we have to walk, because it’s better than walking from the main station.” Sue Furnell said it’s her first time using the station but she’ll definitely be using it more often to get to Addenbrooke’s. The 65-year-old said: “I think it’s brilliant – I don’t drive so the lack of parking wouldn’t really get to me.” Erika Nacario works in Addenbrooke’s and said the station opening has halved her commute from Royston. The 32-year-old said: “It’s very convenient and it’s saved me a lot of time – obviously it can vary in terms of delays, but that’s also the case for the main station. “I don’t drive at all – the one that drives is my fiance, but he works in Papworth so it’s more convenient for him too, it’s horrible traffic from Royston.” Councillor Imogene Blackburn-Horgan, ward councillor for Queen Edith’s which includes Addenbrooke’s Hospital, said it is hoped the well-connected station will reduce “parking stress” and “associated anti-social behaviours”. The Lib Dem councillor said: “With a site that is well supported by train and bus connections it aims to mitigate these issues and support local residents with their wish for more active travel and less traffic. “Being disabled, I have been able to travel via the new Cambridge South Train Station as it is on my doorstep and have found it easy to use the disabled parking, taxi drop-off/pick-up for travelling home and bus connections to reach the city.” Cllr Olaf Hauk, ward councillor for Trumpington, said both Trumpington P&R and Babraham P&R are available for rail commuters, with free parking for up to 18 hours. He said the station was designed primarily for patients, visitors, and staff travelling to the Biomedical Campus and Addenbrooke’s Hospital. He said: “It was not intended to be a starting point for long-distance journeys, which is why it was built without a car park. “People travelling to destinations further afield can use other stations in and around Cambridge, or access Cambridge South by public transport, walking or cycling. “Those who need to drive can use nearby Park & Ride sites, such as Trumpington or Babraham.” He said residents in the nearby Clay Farm and Glebe Farm estates raised concerns about parking after the station’s opening, but their roads are still privately owned by the developer, Vistry, which is responsible for enforcing parking restrictions. Cllr Hauk said: “Motorists who park in breach of those restrictions risk receiving substantial penalty charges. “As local councillors, we will continue to work with Vistry and the councils to ensure that the parking arrangements are fair and effective for both residents and visitors. “At the same time, we remain strong advocates for improving public transport and sustainable travel across Cambridge.” Share

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Travelodge apologise over bedbug outbreak as blogger bitten '100 times'
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary:
Share Share Travelodge have apologised after a travel blogger was bitten 'more than 100 times' by bedbugs. Hannah Stephenson stayed at the Newmarket Road branch of Travelodge in Cambridge on July 26 after a day out with a friend. The 31-year-old said she woke up the following day feeling itchy before discovering her arms were covered in red spots. After investigating her bedding, Hannah said she spotted blood stains and black dots on her pillow before discovering bed bugs crawling in the bedding. Travelodge apologise over bedbug outbreak as blogger bitten '100 times' (Image: Kennedy News/@thecapetownblog) Horrified, Hannah counted 37 bites on her left hand, with more appearing across her arms, chest, back, face and legs throughout the day. Hannah reported the issue to reception but said she was simply told to contact customer services by email and was assured the hotel room wouldn't be let again that night. After calling 111, Hannah was advised to visit a pharmacy where she was given steroid cream and antihistamines to tackle the bites. Hannah posted photos of her bites online, in a video that racked up more than 76,000 views. Although the bites have begun to heal she said they remain visible and now look like chickenpox marks. Travelodge said instances of bed bugs are 'extremely rare' and that housekeeping colleagues are trained to inspect rooms and spot early signs during routine cleaning. The chain confirmed there were bedbugs present in Hannah's room and said they are retraining the housekeeping team at this hotel. Travelodge have apologised to Hannah for the 'distressing' incident and claim they have 'resolved the matter to her satisfaction'. Hannah, from Bassingbourn, Cambridgeshire, said: "I woke up feeling itchy and I started to have lumps forming on my arms. "When I got up, I saw spots of blood on the pillow and black dots. I looked closer and I actually saw a bug on the pillow. "I checked the bedding and they were more in the bedding. As the day went on more and more bites started to emerge. "I counted 37 on my left hand alone but they are too many to count, definitely more than 100, they're really itchy. "I was horrified and shocked. I didn't expect it from a Travelodge, I always thought they are pretty reliable. "I went down to the front desk to check out. I told them and the guy said they wouldn't let out the room again that night and told me to email customer services. "I got a response back saying they will do an investigation, which can last five to eight days. "By the end of the week I was frustrated. I hadn't heard anything and wasn't even offered a refund for my stay. "I wanted to give them a chance to sort it out and a week later I made the video. "I'd like an apology and some compensation because it has caused me a lot of distress. The swelling has gone down. Now it looks like I have chicken pox." Forced to cover the bite marks with foundation while attending her cousin's wedding on August 5, Hannah said she also had to change outfits and wear a dress with long sleeves. Hannah said: "I feel really embarrassed, it's summer so it's not easy to cover them up. I wear long sleeve tops to cover the worst of it. "I felt really embarrassed going to a wedding. They're on my hands, which are hard to cover up, I feel very self-conscious. People are going to think I'm dirty or something. "I don't usually wear foundation but I went to buy one to cover up for the wedding, I couldn't wear my original outfit which had no sleeves. "I was always worrying that someone was going to notice my hands. They have improved but they still look really bad. "People have been horrified, they've said I look like I have a disease. Everyone is saying how bad it looks. Shocked, Hannah said she didn't expect to get bitten at Travelodge after having travelled around the world without an issue. Hannah said: "I don't think I'll ever stay at a Travelodge again. "I want to avoid hotels as much as possible but I can't do that forever. I will always check reviews very closely before I stay anywhere. "Even after a week I am sitting here scratching now. I've travelled everywhere, Africa, South Asia, and I got it in my home town. "I use steroid cream twice a day and take scalding hot showers." A Travelodge spokesperson said: "We are deeply sorry for Ms Stephenson's experience and recognise how distressing an incident like this can be. "The safety of our customers is our priority and we maintain stringent, expert-led measures to prevent and manage pest issues, including training our housekeeping colleagues to be vigilant and to spot early signs wherever possible. "Bed bug activity affects the wider hospitality sector and is completely unrelated to hygiene or cleanliness standards. "In the rare instance that an issue is reported in one of our hotels, we immediately take affected and surrounding
  rooms out of service for inspection and treatment by independent pest control experts. "We have apologised directly to Ms Stephenson and resolved the matter to her satisfaction." Share

Crews have faced challenging conditions and continue to work through long shifts to bring the fire under control. The fire has now been burning for a week straight, but Cambridgeshire Fire and Rescue said that crews are expected to remain at the scene "for the foreseeable future", as the fire is very complex and deep seated. Matthew Warren, chief fire officer at Cambridgeshire Fire and Rescue Service, said: "This has been one of the most significant fires our county has faced in many, many years. "Our crews have been amazing in the face of gruelling conditions. "Every station across the county has been at the site over the course of the week. The blaze covers an area equivalent to around 60 football pitches (Image: Cambridgeshire Fire and Rescue) "Our Control operators have also done an exceptional job in making sure we maintain cover for other emergencies across the county and responding to 999 calls, both from our residents and for other busy services around the country." National Resilience teams and partner agencies are supporting the response. Mr Warren said: "We are extremely grateful to everyone that is pitching in to help. "We’ve seen fire engines here from the length and breadth of the country pitching in to help us tackle the fire, and our partners have been pivotal in our response. "We have also been inundated with refreshment and welfare support from residents and business from across the county. "My sincere thanks goes out to everyone involved." Smoke is expected to remain visible while firefighting operations continue. Residents who feel affected are advised to keep windows and doors closed as a precaution. Share

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Inquest into death of missing man whose remains were found in Wisbech field
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Share Share An inquest into the death of a missing man whose bones were found in a field near Wisbech has concluded. The remains of Sergei Voitechovic, a 34-year-old who had been missing since 2018, were discovered on May 18, 2025, in a field off Lynn Road, Walton Highway, near Wisbech. An inquest into Mr Voitechovic's death was held at Norfolk Coroner’s Court on August 14. Mr Voitechovic was born on August 11, 1990, in Lithuania, and had no history of employment or usual address identified. He had resided in the UK from 2015 until 2017 with periods in and out of the United Kingdom thereafter. He is confirmed to have returned to the United Kingdom on July 11, 2018. The court heard that he had struggled with drug use and gambling, leading to the breakdown of his relationship with his former partner, Agatha Parausete, in 2018. After Mr Voitechovic went missing, his sister Anna reported him to Cambridgeshire Constabulary on October 13, 2018. Neighbours at the time believed he had returned to Lithuania. The court heard that the remains were found by a member of the public in a field known as Richardson Bambers, which had been regularly ploughed and cultivated between 2015 and 2024. The remains of 34-year-old Sergei Voitechovic were discovered in a field off Lynn Road in Walton Highway last year (Image: Chris Bishop) A wallet containing old photographs and a sock containing what appeared to be human bones were found at the scene. Post-mortem testing confirmed they belonged to Sergei Voitechovic. Detective Sergeant Melanie Reid told the court that police found no evidence of third-party involvement in Mr Voitechovic's death. The remains were identified through DNA testing. In her narrative conclusion, assistant coroner Maeve Sykes expressed her condolences to Mr Voitechovic's family and friends. She said it was clear that Sergei was a much-loved son and brother who had his own difficulties which he was trying to work through on his return to the UK on July 11, 2018, shortly after he became a missing person. Ms Sykes added she can only imagine the anguish this has caused her family over the number of years before his remains were identified. Due to the condition and incomplete nature of the remains, the medical cause of death was recorded as unascertained. Share

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Remains of missing Wisbech man found through 'cult offering' discovery, inquest hears
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Share Share The remains of a missing man from Wisbech were discovered by a member of the public who speculated she had stumbled upon a cult offering, an inquest heard. The bones of Sergei Voitechovic, a 34-year-old who had been missing since 2018, were discovered on May 18, 2025, in a field off Lynn Road, Walton Highway, near Wisbech. An inquest into Mr Voitechovic's death was held at Norfolk Coroner’s Court on August 14. The inquest heard that Debbie Garrett was walking to the bus stop from her home on March 1, 2024, when she spotted unusual items at the entrance to a field off Lynn Road. She initially dismissed them as fly-tipping, as the area is known for rubbish dumping, but soon realised one of the items appeared to be a diamond ring. Ms Garrett noticed some items at the entrance to a field just after the roundabout entrance to Lynn Road leading north to Walton Highway. She began to question whether she saw a diamond ring as she continued walking. She later found that the items included jewellery, food, and flowers, and decided to leave them undisturbed. After discussing the discovery with her gardener, Tony, the pair speculated that the items could be part of a cult offering. An inquest into Mr Voitechovic's death was held at Norfolk Coroner’s Court on August 14 (Image: Chris Bishop) They avoided touching or moving anything, and Ms Garrett continued to observe the site during her regular walks. She never saw anyone placing any items or any vehicles in the area, but occasionally heard a flute being played poorly in the middle of the night. In December 2024, Ms Garrett decided to photograph the items to show her aunt. Believing it would be bad luck to touch the offerings, she refrained from moving them and continued her observations. On May 17, 2025, her gardener Tony visited and asked if the offerings were still appearing. The two decided to inspect the site together, and entered the field to examine the items. Ms Garrett picked up a piece of jewellery before putting it down and Tony pointed out a large bone nearby, which they initially believed to be animal remains. As she was leaving, Ms Garrett noticed a sock and picked it up, discovering a wallet inside containing old photographs. Suspecting a possible connection to a body, she returned to the site the following day. She tipped out the contents of the sock and found bones she believed to be part of a human foot. Ms Garrett moved some of the items to make them easier to find and then returned home to call the police. She also researched the value of the jewellery, which she identified as being from H Samuel and each costing £100. Ms Garrett directed police to the site and subsequently found further bones, which she also handed over to officers. She recalled that about two-and-a-half years earlier, a man had been staying in the treeline between the field and Lynn Road. He was described as being of average build, around 5ft 8in tall, and English-speaking. No further offerings have appeared since police attended, but Tony received an image of similar offerings in a field in Tydd St Giles. Share

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Share The family of a former University of Cambridge professor at the centre of a plagiarism row have spoken of their "shock" after his death. Jason Arday, 41, was found "unresponsive" at a property in Battersea, south London, on Friday (August 14). The father-of-two, who became the university's youngest black professor in 2023, was tragically pronounced dead a short while after. A spokesperson for the Metropolitan Police said officers were called by the London Ambulance Service at 3.12pm. It followed a report that a man had been found unresponsive inside a property on Daley Thompson Way, where Arday lived. A spokesperson for the force said: “Sadly, a 41-year-old man was pronounced dead at the scene. “His next-of-kin have been informed and are being supported by officers. “At this time his death is being treated as unexpected, but is not believed to be suspicious. "The case is being investigated by officers from the Met’s Central South Command Unit. A file will be prepared for the coroner." In a heartbreaking tribute, Arday's family said they are “in shock to have lost this amazing father, partner, brother, uncle and son”. They added he had been subjected to "sustained" abuse since he became the institution's youngest black professor in 2023. “The campaign of misinformation was too much for Jason, who was a gentle man and who always wanted to see the best in everyone," they said. "We are in shock to have lost this amazing father, partner, brother, uncle and son. “We won’t comment further at this point beyond asking the press to leave us alone now, and to stop the campaign of harassment which has been waged against Jason and his family for too long.” Cambridge University Vice-Chancellor Professor Deborah Prentice said she had been left "deeply saddened" by Arday's death. She added: "Our heartfelt sympathies go to Jason Arday’s family and friends at this incredibly difficult time.” The news of his passing comes just weeks after Arday was accused of plagiarising from other students for his PhD thesis. On August 5, he resigned as professor of sociology of education at the University of Cambridge. Last week, the university launched an investigation into Arday's appointment and tenure at the institution. Mayor for London Sadiq Khan said Arday's passing was "a tragedy", adding "it should be a wake up call for all of us" For help and support, call the Samaritans for free from a UK phone, completely anonymously, on 116 123 or go to samaritans.org. summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Share Share An investigation has been launched after a two-year-old stray dog was found with "suspected deliberate injuries" hidden beneath its matted fur. Peanut, a Shih Tzu-Lhasa Apso cross was found in Ross Street, Cambridge, on July 2, before he was taken to Woodgreen Pets Charity. When he arrived, concerns were immediately raised about his condition, especially his fur. Peanut's coat was so severely matter that one of his ears became attached to his neck, preventing him from turning his head properly. Woodgreen's veterinary team safely clipped and removed the layers of matted fur. However, they discovered concealed beneath his coat a series of vertical wounds running along his body from his back to his belly. Although the injuries were healing, the pattern and nature of the wounds led the veterinary team to suspect they had been deliberately inflicted. Following his treatment, Woodgreen carried out an investigation into his owner's history. Peanut was found with several unusual wounds believed to have been caused deliberately (Image: RSPCA) This included scanning Peanut's microchip, investigating his previous ownership history and sharing information with the RSPCA. Emma Lyons, veterinary surgeon at Woodgreen Pets Charity, said: "Peanut's condition was one of the worst cases of matting we've seen. "His fur had become so overgrown and tightly knotted that one of his ears was effectively attached to his neck, severely restricting his movement and undoubtedly causing him significant discomfort. "Once we removed the matted coat, we discovered several unusual wounds along one side of his body. "While we cannot say with certainty how they were caused, their appearance is highly concerning and not something we would typically expect to see as the result of an accident. "Our priority was to relieve Peanut's pain, begin treatment and ensure he received the care he so desperately needed." RSPCA animal rescue officer Maya Thakrar, who is investigating the circumstances surrounding Peanut's injuries, said: "The injuries found on Peanut are extremely unusual. Peanut has made remarkable progress during his time at Woodgreen (Image: RSPCA) "Although they were already healing by the time he arrived at Woodgreen, they would have caused him considerable pain. "We are working to establish exactly what happened to Peanut and are particularly keen to speak to anyone who recognises him or knows who cared for him before he was found. "Even the smallest piece of information could prove vital to our investigation." Microchip data suggest Peanut was rehomed approximately six months ago, and the RSPCA is keen to trace the person who took ownership of him at that time. Despite everything he has endured, Peanut has made remarkable progress during his time at Woodgreen. Martina Cohen, dogs team leader at Woodgreen Pets Charity said: "Peanut's resilience has amazed everyone who has cared for him. "Our team feels lucky to have had the chance to watch him grow in confidence during his time with us, and his cheeky personality and zest for life is shining through more and more each day. "It's heartbreaking to think about what he's been through, but thanks to the dedication of our veterinary and care teams, he now has the chance of the happy future every dog deserves." extractedItems.content: Approved updated Highways Asset Management Strategy and winter readiness program. Priority gritting routes across Huntingdonshire and rural connector roads (including B1040) scheduled for pre-winter surface sealing.

extractedItems.title: County Council Children & Young People Committee: SEND Provision & School Transport Update
extractedItems.meetingTitle: Cambridgeshire County Council Children & Young People Committee (14 July 2026)
extractedItems.content: Reported strategic review of Special Educational Needs & Disabilities (SEND) funding allocation. Includes improvements to rural home-to-school transport routes across Huntingdonshire.

extractedItems.title: Parish Council Governance: Highway Contractor Penalties & Flaxon Walk Parking Bay
extractedItems.content: Confirmed that the disabled parking bay at Flaxon Walk was completed that day, ahead of the anticipated timescale. Reported that LGR will affect highway maintenance contractors. Advised that, from September, if highway repairs are carried out to an unsatisfactory standard, councillors should report them to him. New reporting arrangements will be introduced, and contractors may face financial penalties for poor-quality work. Confirmed he is happy to assist by reporting highway issues where necessary.

extractedItems.title: County Council Reports £60m SEND Budget Overspend
extractedItems.content: Reported that Cambridgeshire County Council is forecasting a £60 million overspend on Special Educational Needs and Disabilities (SEND), representing around 50% of the service's budget. Advised that, despite the significant overspend, there has not yet been any noticeable improvement in the service and encouraged councillors to report any specific SEND issues so that they can be raised. Cllr S. White suggested that it may be worthwhile contacting the local school to discuss any SEND-related concerns and gather further information.

extractedItems.title: HDC Local Plan Publication & Autumn Public Consultation
extractedItems.content: Advised that the Local Plan is due to be published in September and encouraged members to submit any comments during the consultation period.

extractedItems.content: Confirmed he will be looking into the future of Newman Stores, including speaking with the owner and liaising with the planning department to help move the matter forward.
